PREFACE 

An acquaintance with Criminal Procedure is likely to be more appreciated by a lawyer after he has come to the bar than before. As a student he is so deeply impressed by the importance of legal doctrines that his preconceptions allow but minor. significance to the manner wherein those doctrines are applied by the courts to actual affairs. His instructors, too, if the curricula of the schools afford safe indication, are apt to be engrossed by the weightier matters of the law and to accord slight consideration to the mint, the anise and the cummin which make the daily routine of the practitioner. Hence the practical conduct of a criminal cause is, not unusually, presented as a scanty appendix or a negligible subsidiary to the substantive law of Crimes.

To one who has been obliged, as most young (and some older) members of the profession are obliged, to try criminal cases, this incidental treatment of the practice in those cases seems much like teaching the preparation of pleadings as incident to the law of Contracts or like expounding the rules of Evidence as ancillary to the law of Negotiable Instruments. It not infrequently results that the youthful, or even the more seasoned, advocate trying a charge of crime is gravely embarrassed by the exiguity and vagueness of his knowledge in one of the most multifarious and most exact branches of his profession, one of which it may well be said that "the study is abstruse and difficult, the occasion sudden and the practice dangerous." An occasional ill fortune of this nature, and some observation, have produced the persuasion that Criminal Procedure is, by reason of its large scope and infinite variety of incidents, entitled to the dignity of an independent subject in the academic curriculum.

Such considerations, together with divers difficulties encountered during some thirty years of instruction in the subject mentioned, have prompted the compilation of the cases here collected. In the selection of them the constant criterion has been the probable needs of the student in his early years of practice. The belief is that most, if not all, of the decisions will prove useful in the ordinary run of criminal litigation, either by way of direct precedent or by analogy. It being obviously impossible to provide for all contingencies, the treatment, both in the cases and in the commentary matter, is addressed to those features of the subject which appear most important or which have been found to present most difficulty to the learner. This seems the extent to which it is profitable to adventure in the time available for iii

iv 

PREFACE 

this course, many minor matters and most local diversities being necessarily pretermitted.

In any legal instruction decided cases are, as is universally agreed, indispensable; and this is preeminently true of instruction in procedural subjects. Accordingly, in this work the effort has been to develop the more substantial doctrines through the adjudications of the courts and to find exfoliation of them in opinions of judges. Yet, necessary as cases are, especially in a so practical branch of the law, the case method of instruction alone, as also is coming to be agreed, is less adapted to procedural subjects than to most others. Experiments running through some years in teaching procedure have confirmed a conviction that, to an adequate understanding of cases, a certain statement of general doctrine and an occasional exposition of a special matter are necessary. Therefore, a not inconsiderable portion of the present volume is given to summaries of the law upon the several heads of Criminal Procedure, these summaries being designed to present concisely the underlying principles upon which the decisions proceed. Of course, such statements do not amount to a treatise upon Criminal Procedure; and the student should be apprised that what is here set out leaves unsaid very much which he ought to know, and he should be advised to acquaint himself with one of the works which develop at large this branch of the law. 

The system of procedure presented in these pages is that which was, until quite recent years, universally accepted in this country and was learned by all lawyers who are now not beyond middle age. 

No attempt has been made to set forth the reformed modes of criminal pleading or the other improvements in practice which have of late been adopted in several jurisdictions or proposed by eminent critics of existing institutions. These alterations have received only casual mention, when adverted to at all. This course has not been prompted by any belief that the traditional practice proceeds always upon the best of all possible principles or that some present usages are beyond betterment. Omission to develop modern amendments is, for one reason, because the older system still, in substance, prevails in much the greater portion of the United States and the substitution of the suggested features is in most States altogether contingent and, to a great extent, apparently improbable; as, in particular, in respect of those incidents which will necessitate changes in the constitutions. 

In addition,. one can hardly understand or at all appreciate a reform unless he knows pretty well what has been or is to be reformed. And to one who values the historical perspective, an acquaintance with certain outmoded methods will appear requisite to any well rounded legal scholarship; even the torch of Omar did not make worthless the treasures of antiquity. Moreover, with all the over-elaboration, rigidity and occasionally exaggerated technicality of the inherited procedure, the candid reader will discern in that system an apprecia-

PREFACE 

tion of settled order and sedulous regularity and also a sanative conservatism, which things cannot wisely be altogether discarded. And such a reader, reflecting upon some lightly proposed reforms, may recall the words of Tertullian, himself a lawyer, in protesting against certain innovations in the forms of worship: "This overthrow of order they call simplicity, and our attention to it they call meretricious embellishment."

WASHINGTON, January, 1939.

I. ARREST 1. Necessity of Arrest. 

Since any violation of the criminal law renders the offender, primarily or by indirection,¹ subject to imprisonment or other corporal punishment, the first step in the prosecution for a crime is to acquire control over the person of the accused. This is ordinarily accomplished by making an arrest, which is defined as "the apprehending or detaining of the person in order to be forthcoming to answer an alleged or suspected crime."

An arrest is made in one of two ways: Either (1) pursuant to a warrant issued by some magistrate and authorising such apprehension of the person, or (2) in certain cases, without a warrant and upon the responsibility of the one making the arrest. 

A. Arrest by Warrant 

2. Magistrates.

In every State are certain officials who are, either by statute or by the unwritten law of the jurisdiction, empowered to authorise the

If the summons is not obeyed, an attachment is issued, upon which the alleged offender is arrested and brought to trial.

The American States adopted only so much of the common law as was suited to their own institutions and conditions. Van Ness v. Pacard, 2 Pet. 137. 

7 L. ed. 374; hence divers common law modes of procedure were generally discarded, as, ex. gr., the use of the ducking-stool. James v. C., 12 S. &

Such are the judges of courts of record, judges of inferior courts having criminal jurisdiction (as police courts), another class of officers generally called justices of the peace, and in some States the mayors, aldermen or other officers of all or certain cities and towns. At common law the coroner had authority to arrest or cause arrest to be made on any charge of felony; though in most (or all) American States such power is exercised by him only in cases of homicide brought before him for inquiry. In addition, the courts of the United States appoint commissioners, who are authorised to investigate offences against Federal law and are commonly known as United States Commissioners." 

Such officials are called magistrates. 

3. The Accusation. 

Upon information duly imparted to a magistrate, affording probable cause to believe that a crime, which is within his jurisdiction, has been committed and that a certain person is guilty thereof, the magistrate may (and in general should¹) prepare and deliver to some proper officer a warrant commanding him to arrest the suspected person. By the common law, it has been said (but also doubted³), a magistrate may thus authorise an arrest upon his own knowledge or upon his private suspicion; which is no doubt true where an offence amounting to felony or a breach of the peace is committed in his

Such a charge is often, perhaps usually, called a complaint; though other names are in various jurisdictions given to it; and the term itself is often applied to accusations which are made for other purposes and which are subject to somewhat different requirements.8 In the absence of a statute prescribing otherwise, the charge need not be made in writing, a merely oral 4. Where the offence charged is one which the magistrate has jurisdiction to try and dispose of, and generally where he has authority to conduct a preliminary hearing and to hold the accused for a higher court, there must be a (more or less) formal charge in writing upon which the trial is to be had; and such charge also is called a complaint: §§ 18, 21, post. The com plaint upon which a warrant is issued need not be so complete or framed in such technical style as the complaint which serves as the basis for trial; the distinction is taken in C. v. Phillips, 16 Pick. 211; S. v. Jones, 88 N. C. 

671; R. v. Croker, 2 Chitty, 138. "The technicalities of an indictment are not requisite in a complaint: Rice v. 

Ames, post, p. 141, citing cases.

In some jurisdictions, however, the cause is tried before the magistrate, and also on appeal before the higher court, upon the charge made to obtain a warrant, and without drawing and filing a further complaint. In such practice, the original charge, or the warrant itself, is the accusation for trial, and corresponds in function to an indictment or information: S. v. 

Jones, 88 N. C. 671. If the first complaint is sufficiently full and positive, the accused may be tried upon it without need of an additional complaint. P. v. Wyatt, 186 N. Y. 383, 79 N. E. 320, 10 L.R.A. (N.S.) 159.

But where the complaint made for arrest is thus to serve for trying the charge, the complaint must be as complete, and almost (or quite) as technically correct as an indictment: 

S. v. Jones, supra; Ex parte Clark, 36 Cal. App. 370, 202 Pac. 50; Lerch v. Sandusky, post, p. 213; Ivey v. S., post, p. 215; §§ 18, 21, post. د.

statement being sufficient to warrant the magistrate in acting.9 But in such case he must exact an oath to the statement,10 and should examine the informant sufficiently to demonstrate probable cause for believing the accused guilty and to insure that the charge is supported by competent evidence.11 

In many (perhaps most) States, however, statutes require that the accusation upon which arrest is to be warranted shall be written and sworn to.12 

A warrant of arrest should not issue except upon the testimony of persons having knowledge of the facts, constituting the crime alleged;13 and a warrant purporting to be issued upon common rumor is invalid. An accusation made by a person professing only information and belief of the facts stated is insufficient to justify the magistrate in directing an arrest.15 If, however, such an accuser state the sources of his information, as an indictment or other public record or the sworn depositions of witnesses, and if he assign the grounds of his belief in such wise as to afford rational inference that his belief is well founded, a charge so made upon information and belief will authorise the issue of a warrant." 16 If a warrant be issued by a magistrate in a case not within his jurisdiction,17 or in disregard of the matters legally prerequisite to authorise that action, the person arrested upon such warrant may recover in trespass for false imprisonment against the magistrate,18 and also against the informant if the latter procured the issue by his own solicitation or direction,19 and against the officer making the arrest, if the irregularity of the warrant is evident upon its face.20 If, however, the warrant, on the face thereof, is

5 valid and purports to have been properly issued, the officer executing it will not be liable, although the other persons concerned may be.21 

If one accused of crime be arrested upon an invalid warrant, or without a warrant or otherwise wrongfully, and is brought before a court, the defect in the warrant or any irregularity in making the arrest will not deprive the court of jurisdiction to try and dispose of the charge.22 The culprit being actually in the presence and powers of the court, his guilt may be adjudicated without inquiry how he was gotten there, and what remedy he may have against those who brought him in is a matter for collateral litigation.23 

4. The Warrant.

The warrant should be addressed to some officer or a class of officers having authority to make arrests.¹ It should recite that complaint upon oath has been preferred to the issuing magistrate, by some person named, charging the accused with a crime specified,2 and should command the officer or officers addressed to arrest the accused and bring him before some judicial functionary, either the issuing magistrate or some other, to be dealt with according to law. 

In some jurisdictions the warrant must be sealed; at common law, 5 Hill, 440; Sandford v. Nicholls, 13

however, the signature of the magistrate sufficiently validates the paper and a seal is unnecessary. 5 The warrant should designate the person to be arrested by his correct name, that is, the surname and at least one Christian name. 

It is not sufficient to indicate the person intended as John Doe or Richard Roe, or by any similar indefinite appellation, unless he is in fact known by such name. If the accused is wholly a stranger, he may be identified by the best description which the nature of the case will allow, as "the man, whose name is unknown, but whose person is well known, and who is employed as the driver of cattle, and wears a badge No. 573." A general warrant, commanding the arrest of the persons who committed a certain crime, as the printers and others concerned in the publication of a specified libel, is void, and those who act upon such authority are liable to any individual arrested pursuant thereto.9

According to the prevailing practice, in some States dictated by statutes 10 and in others by general understanding of the common law, the warrant must specify the offence with which the person to be arrested is charged.¹¹ 

In strict propriety, and necessarily in some jurisdictions, the acts constituting the crime should be set out, with particulars of time, place and other circumstances, very much after the fashion of an indictment.12 Thus, in case of larceny it is recited that a person named has on oath charged that the accused did feloniously steal, take and carry away certain described goods of a specified value, being the property of a designated owner, this being done on a day and at a place mentioned. At common law, however, it is not requisite that any offence at all be specified;18 and where it is desirable to indicate the cause of arrest, the warrant may state only the species of crime, 27 N. B. Arrest without Warrant 

5. Common Law Rules. 

It is always safer and usually desirable that a warrant be obtained before an arrest is made. But conditions often occur in which it is obviously necessary in the interest of society to authorise arrest without the delay and the risk of defeating justice which may be incident to a preparatory proceeding. Therefore, by the common law, which has in different jurisdictions been variously modified by enactments, any one, whether a peace officer or an unofficial person, is justified, in certain circumstances, in arresting another without the authority of a warrant.2

Escaping prisoners may be apprehended without warrant; and it seems immaterial whether the person arrested is charged with felony or misdemeanor, or has been convicted or merely held for trial.18 

Posse Comitatus. A peace officer endeavoring to make an arrest or to suppress a breach of the peace may call upon any person or persons to assist him.19

One so called upon must comply with such request; if he refuses, he is guilty of a misdemeanor.20 If he acts in aid of the officer and an arrest is made, the unofficial person may justify the arrest, even though the officer himself had not actual authority to arrest, provided there was apparent authority for action by the officer.21 Where assistance by the public upon a larger scale is needed, a justice of the peace or the sheriff of the county may summon any number of citizens to join the sheriff in apprehending persons charged with crime or engaged in disorderly conduct; which summoning is called raising the posse comitatus. 

Hue and Cry is an ancient institution of the common law, which consisted in giving alarm to the public of necessity to capture a felon or felons and so collecting a number of citizens to pursue with horns and outcry the persons sought and to arrest them.22 In a proper case hue and cry mightand perhaps still may23-be raised by an officer or by any one else cognisant of the necessity; and private persons who joined in the hue and cry were justified in arresting those who were pursued, although no felony had in fact been committed.

At common law a felony was any offence which occasioned total forfeiture of land and goods: 4 Bl. Com. 

94, 310; Kuntz v. Moffitt, 115 U. S. 

499, 29 L. ed. 458, 6 S. Ct. 148. Though most felonies were punishable by death, capital punishment did not necessarily characterise a crime; since some felonies, such as petty larceny, never caused death, and some misdemeanors were by statute made capital offences without becoming felonies. As forfeitures ceased to be exacted, the old test of felony became less applicable, and it has lately [1915] been declared that the distinction between felony and misdemeanor at common law is "practically impossible of definition:" Chambers v. Burroughs, 44 

App. D. C. 168. "In American law the word [felony] has no clearly defined meaning except as it is given by some statute:" S. v. Setter, 57 Conn. 461, 18 Atl. 782. Mr. John Stuart Mill said: "There is no lawyer who would

treason includes a felony. Any offence which is not a treason or a felony is a misdemeanor.

Statutes in many American States enact that every offence which may be punished capitally or by imprisonment in a penitentiary or State's prison shall be a felony; and a like provision as to offences against the United States is made by an Act of Congress." Several offences which at common law were only misdemeanors—such as libel, perjury, conspiracy-are by statute in many (or most) States made punishable by confinement in a penitentiary. Where, as is true in most jurisdictions, a statute defines a felony as an offence so punishable, the result is, if the statute is to be taken literally, that these former misdemeanors are raised to the degree of felony. 

Whether the principles stated in the last preceding section, relative to arrest without warrant, apply in their full extent under the statutory classification of crimes, is an important question, and one upon which there seems to be no considered adjudication. As felony is defined by the statutes, a person may, in many jurisdictions, be arrested without warrant, by anybody, at any place and at any time of the day or night, upon the charge of publishing a libel or of a past perjury or for having at a former time kept a bawdyhouse or set up a gaming table. Breach of the Peace, as the term is understood with reference to arrests,10 signifies "a disturbance of public order by an act of violence, or by any act likely to produce violence, or which, by causing consternation and alarm, disturbs the peace and quiet of the community." Accordingly, breaches of the peace include¹² assaults, affrays, riots, the forcible entry upon property,13 the discharge of firearms in a public place¹ or elsewhere if apt to cause injury or alarm, the going openly armed in public, shouting in a street15 or (probably) anywhere else if done at an unseasonable hour. It has been said that any public indecorum16 is a breach of the peace, and more specifically that the use of indecent language in the hearing of the public is to be so characterised.17 

On the other hand, an act, though criminal, is not a breach of the cases of felony, be shot and killed: see § 7, post.

It is suggested that, in applying the common law rules respecting arrest for felony without warrant, those rules should be understood as meaning what they meant when they were formulated, and as authorising such arrests only in the cases of those offences which were felonies at that time, and not in cases of those misdemeanors which are made felonies by the statutory classification with reference to punishment in the penitentiary. Something of this kind seems to have been in the mind of the court in Bratton v. U. S., 73 Fed. (2d) 795, where is pointed out what consequences would follow if the common law rules should be applied to such statutory felonies as misprision of felony.

7. Homicide in Arresting.

An officer or other person¹ who has the right to make an arrest, whether with or without warrant, may lawfully use any kind or degree of force which is requisite to accomplish the arrest and to retain possession of the person arrested, even to the extent in some cases of taking the life of that person, where that is necessary to success of the endeavor. With respect to the right to use deadly weapons, such as firearms, the question may be presented in one or more of three aspects.2

Local Modifications. The propositions just stated seem to be well established by the common law. In several of the American States, however, the courts have refused to follow these rules so far as they warrant the taking of life.

Thus, it has been quite extensively held that, when a person actually arrested breaks away, he must not be shot if the charge against him is only of misdemeanor. Even in respect of felonies, there is a disposition in some States to distinguish between those of graver nature, such as murder, rape and perhaps burglary and robbery; and those of less turpitude or less immediate importance to the public safety, like larceny. It is accordingly held that in the latter (not very clearly defined) class of felonies the life of the accused must not be taken when he runs away to avoid or to escape from arrest; and if he is killed, the homicide is manslaughter, if not murder. 10 And in (at necessary to effect arrest, the person so killing is guilty of manslaughter or possibly murder: Birt v. 8. Resistance to Illegal Arrest. 

If an officer or other person undertake to make an arrest without warrant in circumstances which do not justify such action, the one sought to be arrested may rightfully resist to any extent short of taking the life of his assailant.¹ If the resistance results in killing the person endeavoring wrongfully to arrest, his unlawful invasion of the other's right to personal liberty is, at common law, deemed to be such a provocation as will reduce the homicide from murder to manslaughter. If the manner of the attempted arrest reasonably warrants the subject thereof to fear for his life or to apprehend grievous bodily harm, he may be held completely guiltless; but in the ordinary case, where nothing more than a short confinement or like inconvenience can be expected, the killing will be manslaughter. 

9. Search Incident to Arrest. 

An officer or other person, rightfully making an arrest upon a charge of crime, is authorised to search the person of the accused¹ to 

Kinkead, 55 Ark. 502, 18 S. W. 854, 15 L.R.A. 558; Head v. Martin, 85 Ky. 

480, 3 S. W. 622.

Where the line shall be drawn between the grave felonies for which the accused, in running away or breaking away from arrest, may be shot, and those which in this respect rank with misdemeanors, is not altogether clear from the cases. Some of them intimate, if they do not hold, that only those felonies which are capital will justify taking life; at any rate the logic of the opinions runs to that result. It cannot yet be said that these decisions have limited in most States the rules of the common law formulated above.

There is, however, an inevitable confusion arising from the generally prevailing statutory classification of crimes, mentioned in § 6, ante, and making felonies of many offences which at common law and when the rules on this subject were settled, ranked as mere misdemeanors. Although it has been held that the right to kill is the same in case of a statutory felony as of one at common law:

Use in Evidence of Articles Wrongfully Obtained. Where one is wrongfully arrested and things are taken from him, as also in the case where things are obtained in a wrongful search of premises, the question arises, whether such articles may be used in evidence upon the trial of the accused. The general rule is that where physical things are offered in evidence at the trial, the court will not delay the hearing to inquire how they came to the possession of the prosecuting officer;18 though in some jurisdictions, even this principle is subject to certain qualifications.14 If, however, before the trial, the accused represents to the court that articles of his have been improperly acquired and are intended to be offered against him, and prays that they be returned to him, the question so raised is one upon which the authorities are divided and the practice in different jurisdictions is diverse.15 In thirty-one States the evidence, although illegally obtained, is allowed to be used. 16 In the Federal courts and in those of fourteen States such evidence is suppressed upon proof that the rights of the accused were infringed in the acquisition of the articles.17

Although originally limited to the discovery of goods stolen, search warrants may now, either by statutory provisions or by judicial approval, be employed for other purposes, which in some States include finding and seizing articles which have either (1) been used in the commission of a felony, or are (2) intended to be so used, or are (3) possessed in violation of law, or are (4) sought as evidence of guilt for the prosecution of some charge of crime. A search warrant is not primarily or necessarily authority to arrest anybody, but may quite naturally prompt and justify an arrest and prosecution for some crime disclosed by the result of the search; and in the usual form the warrant requires the officer, not only to bring the goods (if found) to the issuing magis-

The use of search warrants is subject to the constitutional restraints which apply to arrests; sec. 3, and note 6 thereto, ante. Accordingly, such a warrant should not issue until a charge has been preferred to the magistrate that a crime has been committed, or that other facts exist which justify search of premises, and that articles subject to seizure are kept in a specified place. This charge must be made upon oath, and must be in the form of a sworn statement which is substantially equivalent to the complaint upon which an arrest is sought, with the addition of appropriate averment concerning the existence and location of the goods to be looked for. The contents, and sometimes even the wording, of such statements are in some States prescribed by statutes, which differ in respect of details in various States; and whatever be the statutory form, it must be accurately followed. general, the applicant for a warrant must either directly declare that a crime has been committed or that some other fact exists which justifies search, or must swear to facts which, in the judgment of the magistrate, constitute probable cause to believe the existence of matters which make search permissible.9

In What facts constitute such probable cause is a question of law, which is, in the first instance, to be determined by the magistrate; but his ruling is subject to revision, and the sufficiency of the sworn statement to authorise issue of a warrant may be judicially examined for the purpose of adjudging the validity of the warrant." 21 to probable cause are returned to the former possessor and cannot be used against him. 12 The existence of probable cause cannot, it has been said, be determined by any fixed formula, but depends upon the elements of the particular case,¹ and the numerous rulings upon the point are not always readily reconcilable. 

The general definition of probable cause which has been cited in connection with arrests (sec. 5, note 6, ante), no doubt applies to these cases;1 .13 but the application to an actual predicament of facts is often controlled by special circumstances which differentiate cases of similar content. Mere suspicion, it is universally agreed, does not amount to probable cause; 14 but how strong and reasonable must be the suspicion, and how persuasive should be the suspicious circumstances to create probable cause, is a question upon which, in like conditions, judges often disagree.15 

The warrant should recite that a proper complaint has been made before the issuing magistrate by some designated person, and should direct the officer to search certain premises for certain specific goods, which being found, he must bring to the magistrate for disposal as the facts to be proved shall make lawful.16 The place to be searched must be specified and so described that it may be identified, a general warrant authorising search of all and any places being void.17 The articles sought also must be described, and it is not sufficient to designate them generally as goods, wares and merchandise or by like indefinite nomenclature.18 The warrant must be executed in the daytime, though in certain cases for special reasons search in the night may be expressly authorised.19 The officer must take only such articles as his warrant mentions; if he takes others, he becomes a trespasser.20

Caudle v. Seymour, 1 Q. B. 889, 113 Eng. Reprint, 1372..

Queen's Bench. 1841. 

Seymour was a magistrate, and to him it was represented that Caudle had injured a girl named Warner by bad surgical treatment. 

Seymour's clerk interviewed the girl and took her sworn statement of the facts, and upon reading this statement, Seymour issued a warrant for the arrest of Caudle. The warrant did not recite any complaint made upon oath, but directed Caudle to be arrested "to answer to all such matters and things as shall be objected against him on oath by Mary Ann Warner for an assault committed on her" at Brighton on the 24th of August, 1839. On this warrant

Caudle was arrested, tried on a charge of assault, and acquitted; whereupon he brought this action against the magistrate for false imprisonment. There was a verdict for Caudle, which the court on a motion for new trial held to be correct.

COLERIDGE, J.: It is true that a magistrate here has jurisdiction over the offence in the abstract; but to give him jurisdiction in any particular case it must be shown that there was a proper charge upon oath in that case. A man has no right, because he is a magistrate, to order another to be taken for an offence over which he has jurisdiction without a charge regularly made.

A magistrate has no jurisdiction in such a case as this without a charge on oath. 

The warrant here does not state a charge; and the facts independent of the warrant do not show such a charge on oath as justifies. 

LORD DENMAN, C. J.: The warrant is clearly insufficient. It does not state any information on oath or that the fact was really committed. But then it is said that although the warrant was irregular, the justice was still protected against an action of trespass, having as a magistrate jurisdiction over the offence. But his protection depends, as my brother Coleridge has observed, not on jurisdiction over the subject matter, but jurisdiction over the individual arrested. 

To give him that jurisdiction, there should have been an information properly laid. 

PATTESON, J.: The every-day practice is to state an information on oath; if the magistrate omits that, he must take the consequence. 

Comfort v. Fulton, 36 Barbour, 56. Supreme Court of New York. 1861.

To Soules, who was a justice of the peace, Fulton presented a written complaint alleging that some potatoes of his had been stolen and that he had reason to suspect that Comfort had stolen them. Upon oral examination by the justice, Fulton said that his reason for suspecting Comfort was that a son of Fulton had seen Comfort dig some potatoes from Fulton's land and carry them away. On this evidence Soules issued a warrant for the arrest 

Messenger, 2 B. & P. 158. So if he takes goods not the property of the accused: Owens v. Way, 141 Ga. 796, 82 S. E. 132.

PECKHAM, J.: The Constitution of the United States provides that "no warrant shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized." Art. 4. do not know why this is not the law of the land in State as well as in United States tribunals. It is in terms reenacted in our bill of rights. 1 R. S. 93.

In this case information from his son, by the complainant, was no proof whatever. It cannot be by possibility "probable cause supported by oath." 

It is no "oath" or affirmation within the meaning of the law. 

Had any fact been stated, so as to enable the magistrate to exercise his judgment as to the probable cause, he could not be liable for an error in its exercise. Here was nothing more (nor so much in fact) than if the son had come into court and stated, without oath, that he saw the plaintiff commit the offence. 

That would not be claimed to be sufficient. 

The Queen v. Hughes, L. R. 4 Q. B. Div. 614. Queen's Bench Division. 1879. 

A subordinate clerk in the office of the clerk to the justices of petty sessions issued to Hughes a form of a warrant directing the arrest of one Stanley on the charge of assaulting Hughes. There was no written information or oath made by Hughes or by any one else upon which to found such a warrant, but Hughes took the paper to a magistrate and procured him to sign it. On this warrant Stanley was arrested, brought to trial before a court composed of magistrates, defended himself without objecting to the validity of the warrant, and was convicted, Hughes giving testimony on oath against him.

Afterward Hughes was indicted upon the charge that he had committed perjury in his testimony at the trial of Stanley, and upon this indictment Hughes was found guilty.

At the trial of Hughes, the facts appearing as here stated, his counsel contended that the court which tried Stanley was without jurisdiction of the case because the proceeding was void by reason of the irregular way wherein Stanley had been arrested and brought before the court; wherefore (it was inferred) Hughes could not be guilty of perjury by swearing falsely before magistrates having no jurisdiction in the matter tried before them. This point being certified by Bramwell, L. J., to the court considering crown cases reserved, that court affirmed the conviction, three of the judges delivering quite elaborate opinions upon the question presented.¹

LOPES, J.: I think the warrant in this case [of Stanley] was mere process for the purpose of bringing the party complained of before the justices, and had nothing whatever to do with the jurisdiction of the justices. I am of opinion that whether Stanley was summoned, brought by warrant, came voluntarily, was brought by force, or under an illegal warrant, is immaterial; being before the justices, however brought there, the justices, if they had jurisdiction, in respect of time and place, over the offence, were competent to entertain the charge; and being so competent, a false oath, willfully taken, in respect of something material, would be perjury. 

HAWKINS, J.: I have assumed as a fact, from the case stated, that Stanley was arrested and brought before the justices upon as illegal a warrant as ever was issued. A warrant signed by a magistrate, not only without any written information or oath to justify it, but without any information at all. It follows that the magistrate who issued the warrant, and the defendant who with knowledge of its illegality executed it, were liable to an action for false imprisonment. 

Wrongful, however, as the proceedings were by which Stanley was brought into the presence of the magistrates to answer a charge which up to that moment had never been legally preferred against him, before those magistrates and in his presence a charge was made over which, if duly made, they had jurisdiction. Upon that charge it was that the hearing proceeded; and in support of that charge it was that the defendant was sworn, and in giving his evidence, swore corruptly and falsely. 

People v. Miller, 235 Mich. 340, 209 N. W. 81. Supreme Court of Michigan. 1926.

Irma Miller was arrested whilst soliciting in a public street, which was a statutory misdemeanor. Upon a trial, she was convicted, and the judgment was affirmed.

CLARK, J.: Defendant, on error, contends that her arrest without warrant was illegal, for the reason that, if offending, she was guilty of but a misdemeanor and was taken in no breach of the peace. The arrest was followed by complaint and warrant, under which she was held. It is not urged that the evidence against her was obtained by or because of the arrest. The contention is, barely, that she should have been discharged because the arrest was illegal.

Defendant was charged and held on complaint and warrant that are regular. In the trial itself she suffered no prejudice, and was deprived of no right to which she was lawfully entitled, because of the arrest. If the arrest was irregular, she was not thereby given the right to say that she should not be tried at all. Ker v. Illinois, 119 U. S. 436, 30 L. ed. 421, 7 S. Ct. 

225; 16 Corp. Juris, p. 175; In re Little, 129 Mich. 454, 89 N. W. 38, 57 

L.R.A. 295. brought before him, though in an irregular and informal manner, was more fully and elaborately discussed than in the case of Reg. v. Hughes,

L. R. 4 Q. B. Div. 614."

Commonwealth v. Crotty, 10 Allen, 403, 87 Am. Dec. 669.

Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts. 1865. 

Crotty and others were indicted upon a charge of riot, supposed to be committed by resisting an officer who attempted to arrest Crotty. 

At the trial the district attorney proved that one Peaslee had made a complaint to a police court charging that "John Doe or Richard

Roe, whose other or true name is to your complainant unknown," had committed an assault and battery upon him; upon which complaint a warrant, which was attached to the complaint, was issued against "John Doe or Richard Roe, whose other or true name is to your complainant unknown, named in the foregoing complaint." Neither the complaint nor the warrant contained any further description or means of identification of the person to be arrested. Upon this warrant, a deputy sheriff with assistants proceeded to arrest Morris Crotty, one of the present defendants, as the real person chargeable. 

Crotty resisted the arrest on the ground that the warrant was invalid, and the other defendants aided him. The officer testified that he did not rely upon any description in the warrant, but upon information otherwise obtained, for the identification of Crotty.

The judge instructed the jury that the above warrant authorised the arrest of Crotty, provided he was the person accused in the complaint attached to the warrant, notwithstanding the complaint or warrant did not contain his name, any description of his person, or any statement of the reason why his person was not described, and notwithstanding the person accused was described as "John Doe or Richard Roe;" and that Crotty's assault upon and resistance of the officer were unlawful acts, and if Crotty, or either of the defendants with him, and with other persons, or said Crotty with other persons to the number of three or more in all, mutually assisted each other in assaulting and resisting said officer while attempting to arrest Crotty under said warrant, and they acted in a violent and tumultuous manner, such persons were guilty of a riot. 

The jury returned a verdict of guilty against some of the defendants, and they alleged exceptions.

BIGELOW, C. J. We cannot entertain a doubt that the warrant on which the officer attempted to arrest one of the defendants at the time of the alleged riot was insufficient, illegal and void. It did not contain the name of the defendant, nor any description or designation by which he could be known and identified as the person against whom it was issued. It was in effect a general warrant, upon which any other individual might as well have been arrested, as being included in the description, as the defendant himself. Such a warrant was contrary to elementary principles, and in direct violation of the constitutional right of the citizen, as set forth in the Declaration of Rights, art. 14, which declares that every subject has a right to be

secure from all unreasonable searches and seizures of his person, and that all warrants, therefore, are contrary to this right, if the order in the warrant to a civil officer to arrest one or more suspected persons or to seize their property be not accompanied with a special designation of the persons or objects of search, arrest or seizure. 

This is in fact only a declaration of an ancient common law right. It was always necessary to express the name or give some description of a party to be arrested on a warrant; and if one was granted with the name in blank, and without other designation of the person to be arrested, it was void. 1 Hale P. C. 577, 2 Ib. 119. Foster, 312. 

7 Dane Ab. 248. 1 Chit. Crim. Law, 39. Mead v. Hawes, 7 Cow. 

332, and cases cited.

This rule or principle does not prevent the issue and service of a warrant against a party whose name is unknown. In such case the best description possible of the person to be arrested is to be given in the warrant; but it must be sufficient to indicate clearly on whom it is to be served, by stating his occupation, his personal appearance and peculiarities, the place of his residence, or other circumstances by which he can be identified. 1 Chit. Crim. Law, 39, 40.

The warrant being defective and void on its face, the officer had no right to arrest the person on whom he attempted to serve it. He acted without warrant and was a trespasser. The defendant whom he sought to arrest had a right to resist by force, using no more than was necessary to resist the unlawful acts of the officer. An officer who acts under a void precept, and a person doing the same act who is not an officer, stand on the same footing; Shadgett v. Clipson, 8 

East, 328; Rex v. Hood, 1 Mood. C. C. 281; Hoye v. Bush, 2 Scott 

N. R. 86; Pearce v. Atwood, 13 Mass. 324, 344; Sanford v. Nichols, Ib. 286; Commonwealth v. Kennard, 8 Pick. 133; and any third person may lawfully interfere to prevent an arrest under a void warrant, doing no more than is necessary for that purpose. 1 Chit. Crim. 

Law, 44. The King v. Osmer, 5 East 304-308. 

The defendants, therefore, in resisting the officer in making an arrest under the warrant in question, if they were guilty of no improper or excessive force or violence, did not do an unlawful act by lawful means, or a lawful act by unlawful means, and so could not be convicted of the misdemeanor of a riot, with which they are charged in the indictment.

The instructions under which the case was submitted to the jury did not meet this aspect of the case. It must therefore go to a new trial.¹

78, 38 L. ed. 643, 14 S. Ct. 752, Cases on Torts, 103.

In Re Chandless, 110 N. J. Eq. 527, 160 Atl. 670. Court of 

Chancery, New Jersey. 1930.

Chandless was arrested by the sheriff of Bergen county upon a warrant issued by a justice of the Supreme Court, addressed to the sheriff, and reading "We command you that you attach and arrest Ralph W. Chandless, so that you have him before me, Charles W. 

Parker, Justice of the Supreme Court, at [a specified place and time], to answer unto me for certain trespasses and unlawful acts lately done and committed by him." Upon a writ of habeas corpus obtained by Chandless from a vice chancellor, the sheriff produced the prisoner and returned that he was held in virtue of the warrant issued by Justice Parker. The petitioner was discharged. 

FALLON, V. C.: It is clearly manifest from the sheriff's return to the writ of habeas corpus that the warrant which he sets forth as the cause of the petitioner's detention or confinement is insufficient in law to justify same. The warrant does not state grounds upon which the petitioner was arrested and taken in custody by the sheriff. 

It is elementary that a warrant under and by virtue of which a citizen is to be arrested, detained in custody, and thus deprived of his liberty, must state the grounds upon which the arrest is to be made. 

It must set forth an offence against the law or a violation of law charged against the person named in the warrant as the offender, and, if the warrant be issued as a mesne process in a civil action it should set forth the particulars of the demand his arrest was effected to answer. The warrant in question requires the sheriff to arrest the petitioner and have him before Justice Parker to answer unto him "for certain trespasses and unlawful acts lately done and committed by him." No offence against the law or violation of law is charged for which the petitioner might lawfully be arrested, placed in custody of the sheriff, and thus deprived of his liberty. The warrant is novel, vague, and uncertain, and reciting, as it does, "certain trespasses and unlawful acts," is multitudinous. It does not inform the alleged offender of an offence against the law or violation of law with which he is charged. The "certain trespasses and unlawful acts" stated may properly be considered by the court in the matter sub judice as conclusions without basis in fact. There are many trespasses and violations of law for which a citizen may not be amenable to arrest and imprisonment. Warrants, and complaints upon which warrants are founded, must set forth an offense against the law or violation of the special designation that the Constitution requires:" Harwood v. Siphers, 70 Me. 464. 

In 1822 an unknown prisoner who refused to give his name was, by the advice of the judges, indicted as "a person whose name is unknown, but who was personally brought before the [grand] jurors by the keeper of the prison: " Rex v. 

Russ. & 

Ry. 489. But Mr. Bishop observes that this mode of identification might not suffice in a warrant of arrest: 1 

Bishop Crim. Proc. sec. 676.

law with which an alleged offender is charged. In Summit v. Hahr, 66 N. J. Law, 333, 52 A. 956, our Court of Errors and Appeals held a complaint which was intended to set forth a violation of a city ordinance which forbade the selling or offering for sale of intoxicating liquors on Sunday, and which charged that the accused sold and offered for sale such liquors "on June 10th, 17th, and 24th and 

July 1st, and on divers other Sundays, A. D. 1900, and for a long time prior thereto," to be defective, vague, and uncertain, and that an accused person should not, especially in summary proceedings, be required to meet so multitudinous a charge. 

It was sought at the hearing on the return of the writ of habeas corpus to have me look beyond the return, with a view of obtaining information as to the reasons which prompted the Supreme Court justice to issue the warrant hereinabove referred to. I stated to counsel that I was not empowered so to do, and that only the return to the writ, and the validity and the sufficiency of the warrant on its face mentioned therein as the authority for the sheriff to hold the petitioner in custody, could be inquired into on habeas corpus to justify the detention of the petitioner. Such I understand to be the rule of law. The matter sub judice is distinguishable from a case in which one is held in custody under warrant of commitment issued by a magistrate or other proper officer on an accusation of crime. 

The petitioner should be discharged from custody. 

Burns v. Erben, 40 N. Y. 463. Court of Appeals, New York. 1869. 

WOODRUFF, J.: By section 8 of the act to establish a Metropolitan Police District, passed April 15th, 1857 (chap. 569 of Laws of 

1857), the members of the police force of that district are given "in every part of the state of New York, all the common law and statutory powers of constables, except for the service of civil process. 

And in the amendatory act passed April 10, 1860 (chap. 259 of

Laws of 1860), it is declared in the 28th section, that the members of the police force of that district "shall possess in every part of the State all the common law and statutory powers of constables, except for the service of civil process."

In pursuance of information given by the defendant, Erben, the defendant, Frost, accompanied by Erben, arrested the plaintiff without a warrant, took her to the police station, where she was detained a few minutes, and after some conversation with the officer in charge, she was permitted to return to her residence. For this she has brought the present action for false imprisonment.

A felony had been committed that evening, at the house of Mr. 

Henry Erben, the defendant's father. On that point there is no dispute or conflict. The plaintiff had visited the house that evening, and, according to the information upon which the defendant acted.

ARREST 

29 was the only person not a member of the family, who had been in the basement. Silver had been stolen from the basement. It was there when the plaintiff entered and until after 8 o'clock: and it was missed very shortly after she left the house. Of these facts the proof was distinct and without contradiction.

Upon a report of these facts, Frost, accompanied by the defendant, Erben, made the arrest as above stated. 

The inquiry is, therefore, whether under the statutes above cited and the common law rule in respect of arrests made or aided by private persons, the plaintiff was entitled to recover. There were no facts in dispute requiring the submission of any question to the jury, unless it be held that there was no justification. 

I have no doubt upon the subject. The writers upon criminal law and the reported cases, so far as I have examined them, hold uniform language. 

Lord Tenterden, Ch. J., in Beckwith v. Philby (6 Barn. & Cres., 735), says: "The only question of law in this case is, whether a constable, having a reasonable cause to suspect that a person has committed a felony, may detain such persons until he can be brought before a justice of the peace to have his conduct investigated. There is this distinction between a private individual and a constable; in order to justify the former in causing the imprisonment of a person, he must not only make out a reasonable ground of suspicion, but he must prove that a felony has actually been committed; whereas a constable having reasonable ground to suspect that a felony has been committed, is authorised to detain the party suspected until inquiry can be made by the proper authorities." (See Hawk P. C., book 2, chap. 12, 13; 1 Russell on Crime, 594, 5; Steph. Cr. L. 242, 3; 1 Chit. 

Cr. L., 15, 17; Samuel v. Payne, Doug. 358; Lawrence v. Hedger, 3 

Taunt., 14; Regina v. Toohy, 2 Ld. Raymond, 130; Hobbs v. 

Brandscomb, 3. Camp., 420; Davis v. Russell, 5 Bing., 354; Cowles v. Dunbar, 2 Car. and P., 565.) The justification of an arrest by a private person was made in Allen v. Wright (8 Carr and Payne, 522), to depend on first, the fact that a felony had been actually committed; and second, that the circumstances were such that a reasonable person, acting without. passion and prejudice, would have fairly suspected the plaintiff of being the person who did it. These principles are affirmed in this State in Mix v. Clute (3) 

Wend., 350), in very distinct terms. "If a felony has been committed by the person arrested, the arrest may be justified by any person without warrant. If an innocent person is arrested upon suspicion by a private individual, such individual is excused if a felony was in fact committed, and there was reasonable ground to suspect the person arrested. But if no felony was committed by any one, and a private individual arrest without warrant, such arrest is illegal,

though an officer would be justified if he acted upon information from another which he had reason to believe." 

The fact being proved in this case that a felony had in fact been committed, I have no hesitation in saying that, however unfortunate it was to the plaintiff, the circumstances fully justified the suspicion which led to her arrest. It is claimed that these circumstances should have been submitted to the jury. Not so; a verdict finding no reasonable ground of suspicion would have been against evidence. There was no conflict of testimony, and that the arrest was made without malice, in good faith, and upon reasonable grounds, is to my mind incontrovertible. 

Mangino v. Todd, 19 Ala. App. 486, 98 So. 323. Court of Appeals, Alabama. 1923.

Under circumstances set forth in the sequent opinion, Mangino was shot by a deputy sheriff named Malone. This action was brought by Mangino against the sheriff, Todd, and the surety in his official bond. A judgment had by the defendants was reversed. 

BRICKEN, P. J.: It was contended by the defendants that if the plaintiff was shot by a deputy sheriff, as alleged in his complaint, such shooting was done in self-defense.

Counsel for the appellees state the facts of their defense in brief as follows: 

"The sheriff's posse went out on the morning of May 21, 1921, to raid a still, which they did, and, after doing so were waiting by the roadside near where the still had been raided. They heard a conveyance coming, and, as one of the witnesses said, they thought it was one of the wildcatters 'getting away with the booze.' The men in the buggy looked like the men that the deputies were after, and, when the deputies undertook to halt the buggy to ascertain if they were the men that they were after, the men in the buggy whipped up the mule and one of them raised up and pulled what the deputies took to be a pistol from his pocket. Thereupon the deputies fired. 

That the men threw a bottle of whisky from the buggy and kept driving. One of these men in the buggy was the plaintiff, who got shot. 

The officers believed that the plaintiff and his companion were the men who had been making whisky. That the plaintiff was some five or ten miles from his home at two o'clock in the morning. That the plaintiff and his companion were violating the prohibition law, in that they had a bottle of whisky, even if they had not been manufacturing it." In order to justify an arrest without a warrant, the person arrested, or sought to be arrested, must either have committed a public offense or threatened a breach of the peace in the presence of the arresting officer; or a felony must have been committed, though not

ARREST 

31 in the presence of the officer, by the person arrested; or a felony must have been committed and the officer must have reasonable cause to believe that the person arrested, or sought to be arrested, committed such felony, or the officer must have reasonable cause to believe that the person arrested, or sought to be arrested, has committed a felony; or a charge upon reasonable cause must be made that the person arrested has committed a felony. 

Under the proof in this case, it is without dispute that the officers who attempted to halt the plaintiff and his companion had no warrant for their arrest or for the arrest of either of them. According to the testimony of the witness Will West, said witness and Sid Malone and Curtis Malone, all deputy sheriffs, were together at the house of one At Bishop. It appears that the two Malones were sent by the sheriff of Franklin county to assist the witness Will West in making a raid; that the witness West made the raid alone but did not completely destroy the still which he raided, and that these deputies decided to go back and complete the destruction of the still; that while they were getting ready to start, waiting for one Lawler to come with a car, they heard a buggy coming along and that someone made inquiry to know what it meant; that he, West, said, "I guess that is some of them fellows getting out from over there, they are getting away with the booze." The witness testified that he meant several persons named but who did include the plaintiff or his companion; that thereupon Mr. Malone stated that they had better go down and see about them, and that they walked on down to the road and thought it was two of the persons for whom the officers were looking and that it looked very much like them; that Sid Malone asked 

West to step out in the road and halt the persons driving in the buggy, which he did, and that thereupon the young man who was driving rose up and jerked the lines and slapped the mule and when the witness caught at the mule he was run over, knocked down, and pushed aside; that when he got on his feet the buggy was going on up the road some distance; and that the only persons at the roadside were the deputy sheriffs.

The testimony is without dispute that, at the time the officers attempted to halt the plaintiff and his companion, neither the plaintiff nor his companion had committed any offense in the presence of any of the officers, of which the officers were cognizant. It is therefore without dispute that the sole justification for the attempt on the part of the deputy sheriff to halt the plaintiff and his companion as they drove along the public highway was that officer West guessed that the plaintiff and his companion were hauling prohibited liquors from the still which had been destroyed, and were probably some of the parties for whom they had warrants. The hour was around two o'clock in the morning. It does not appear from the testimony of any of the officers that there was sufficient light to enable them to tell who the travelers were. The plaintiff and his com-

panion testified that a flash light was used by one of the officers, which frightened the mule, thus causing the officer West to be knocked down.

Section 5 of the Constitution of Alabama provides in effect that the people shall be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and possessions from unreasonable seizure or searches. Even if the deputy sheriffs had been informed that the plaintiff and his companion were hauling prohibited liquors along the public highway, they would have had no right to have seized and searched the plaintiff and his companion, except through the instrumentality of a legal warrant, or unless they knew of their knowledge that the plaintiff and his companion were then and there transporting prohibited liquors in their presence. No lawful arrest in this case was ever made or attempted to be made. In fact, under the evidence in this case, it appears that the officers did not intend to arrest the person in the buggy unless, after halting the buggy, they should find prohibited liquors therein, or should find that the travelers were two of the persons for whom they had warrants. It is quite clear that the officers had no legal right to halt the buggy without a warrant for the purpose of ascertaining whether or not it contained prohibited liquors. 

The sole inquiry is therefore whether or not said officers had the right to halt a buggy containing the plaintiff and his companion, who then were not charged with any offense and who then, in so far as said officers had actual knowledge, had committed no offense in their presence, to enable said officers to ascertain whether or not the plaintiff and his companion were two persons for whom said officers had warrants. And this inquiry is dependent upon whether or not the officers had probable cause to believe that the buggy which they heard approaching contained one or more persons for whose arrest they had warrants. The witness West testified he stated in the presence of the other officers, "I guess that is some of them fellows getting out from over there, they are getting away with the booze," and this statement was made in reply to the question, "What do you reckon that means?" That thereupon Mr. Malone said, "We had better go down and see about them;" that after reaching the road "Sid asked me to step out in the road and halt them and I did." The witness 

Sid Malone corroborated the statement made by West with reference to his guess except he testified that West said that he "guessed that was Porter and Baty now making a getaway," and that West further said, "Let's go out and stop them"-which declarations all show that at best the officers entertained the suspicion that the occupant, or occupants, might be one or more of the persons for whom they had warrants, and that, in order to determine whether this was true or not, they would have to stop the buggy and make an inspection of said occupants. But the officers had no legal right to halt the buggy under these circumstances, for the mere suspicion and belief of the officers, it matters not how intensely and honestly the same were en-

ARREST 

33 tertained, did not constitute probable cause unless the belief was founded upon facts then known to the officers which would have justified a reasonable and cautious man in believing that the occupants of the buggy were persons for whom said officers held warrants of arrest. Now what were the facts upon which such honest belief could have been founded at the time the officers went to the road for the purpose of halting the buggy? A still had been raided earlier in the night by West; he saw no one at the still; they heard a buggy coming down the road from the direction in which the still was located at a very early hour in the morning. Can these facts induce a mind seeking the truth to reach the conclusion that a reasonable and prudent man would have determined that the buggy contained one or more persons for whom the officers had warrants of arrest? We think not. Suspicion and belief not founded upon facts are insufficient. Lunsford v. Dietrich, 93 Ala. 565, 9 South. 308, 30 Am. St.

Rep. 79. What the effort of the officers disclosed with respect to the plaintiff and his companion after the effort to halt them is immaterial. It was not upon the facts disclosed by the effort to halt the buggy that the officers reached the determination to halt it, and the fact that one of the occupants sprang up and drew a pistol, or something that looked like a pistol, is immaterial for such last-named act was occasioned by the unlawful effort of the officers to halt the buggy. "An illegal arrest cannot be justified by facts subsequently ascertained; nor can an arrest made for one purpose be justified for another." Cunningham v. Baker, 104 Ala. 160, 16 South. 68, 53 Am. 

St. Rep. 27.

The very same facts and authorities would obtain in the event the officers should have attempted to justify the arrest of the plaintiff and his companion, upon the theory that a felony had been committed, and they had reasonable cause to believe the plaintiff and his companion had committed it, because, in either and all contingencies, the officers must have acted upon an honest belief founded upon a reasonable cause which existed at the time they embarked upon their enterprise that is, at the time they first heard the buggy coming down the road.

The fact that the occupants of the buggy may have been conveying prohibited liquors is immaterial. This fact could not have been known to the officers at the time they attempted to make the arrest in so far as the evidence in this case discloses and would not have justified, therefore, the effort to halt the buggy. Cobb v. State, 19 

Ala. App. 345, 97 South. 779; Ex parte Stewart Cobb, 210 Ala. 252, 97 South. 783.

The further fact that the plaintiff and his companion fled from the officers, while transporting intoxicating liquors, could not and did not justify the officers firing their pistols at and towards the fleeing misdemeanants, although they could not otherwise be overtaken. 

[Cases in Crim. Proc.]-3

Williams v. State, 44 Ala. 41; Davis v. State, 92 Ala: 20, 9 South. 

616; Angling v. State, 137 Ala. 17, 34 South. 846; Handley v. State, 96 Ala. 48, 11 South. 322, 38 Am. St. Rep. 81; Birt v. State, 156 

Ala. 29, 46 South. 858; Suell v. Derricott, 161 Ala. 259, 49 South. 

895, 23 L.R.A. (N.S.) 996, 18 Ann. Cas. 636; Cobb v. State, supra.

The Supreme Court of Mississippi in the case of State v. Cunningham said: "We unqualifiedly condemn this practice of the reckless use of firearms. Officers should make all reasonable efforts to apprehend criminals; but this duty does not justify the use of firearms, except in the cases authorized by law. Officers, as well as other persons, should have a true appreciation of the value of a human life." State v. Cunningham, 107 Miss. 140, 65 South. 115, 51 L.R.A.(N.S.) 1179. 

The defense of self-defense does not and cannot exist in this case because the plaintiff and his companion were running away at the time the plaintiff received his wound. The evidence is without dispute that plaintiff offered no resistance whatever and that the bullet entered his leg from the rear. Therefore the plea of self-defense upon the part of the deputy sheriffs cannot avail the defendants. Angling v. State, supra; Maughon v. State, 7 Ga. App. 660, 67 S. E. 

842; 2 R. C. L. 473, § 30. Cobb v. State, supra.

Should it be conceded that the plaintiff's companion drew a pistol at the time the officer West attempted to halt the buggy, such fact would not have justified the officers in shooting at the plaintiff and his companion under the doctrine of self-defense, because the effort to halt the buggy was illegal and unauthorized in law and was the factor which led up to the drawing of the weapon, if it was in fact drawn, by the companion of the plaintiff. The deputy sheriffs were, therefore, not free from fault and the plea of self-defense cannot be interposed unless they were free from fault. 

It is immaterial which one of the three officers fired the shot that produced the wound. They were all engaged upon a common enterprise or adventure which contemplated the halting of the buggy and its occupants. They were present, encouraging, aiding, and abetting each other in this enterprise, and they were all equally responsible with whichever one of them actually fired the shot that produced the wound. Tanner v. State, 92 Ala. 1, 9 South. 613.

Upon an indictment alleging various violations of the law against gaming, Zerega was convicted and sentenced to confinement in a jail for six months. This conviction was afirmed.

BRADBURY, C. J.: The authority of peace officers to arrest with out a warrant from a magistrate is a subject that has received the attention of the courts and text-writers from an early period in the history and development of the common law in both England and America. Some of the earlier English authorities, while the prerogatives of the government were more highly considered than at a later day, maintained the power. (2 Hale P. C. 90.) But even

then the doctrine met with a resistance which finally overturned it. (1 East P. C. 305.) Regina v. Tooley, 2 Lord Raymond, 1301, where Lord Holt, in delivering the opinion of the majority of the court, is reported as saying: "The prisoners in this case had sufficient provocation; for if one be imprisoned upon an unlawful authority, it is a sufficient provocation to all people out of compassion; much more where it is done under a color of justice, and where the liberty of the subject is invaded, it is a provocation to all the subjects of England. He said, that a constable cannot arrest, but when he sees an actual breach of peace, and if the affray be over, he can not arrest." See also 2 Hawk. Crim. Law, 13, Sec. 8. The later English authorities seem to settle the law there in accordance with the views of Lord Holt. Coupey v. Henley, et al., 2 Esp. 540; 

Baynes v. Brewster, 2 A. & E. (N. S.) 375; Regina v. Mable, 9 C. & P. 474; Timothy v. Simpson, 1 C. M. & R. 757; Grant v. Moser, 5 Mann. & G. 123; 1 Russ. on Cri. (8th ed.) 410, 805. In the case of Cook v. Nethercote, 6 C. & P. 741, Alderson, B., in summing up says: "If, however, there has been an affray, and that affray were over, then the constable had not and ought not to have the power of apprehending the persons engaged in it; for the power is given him by law to prevent a breach of the peace; and where a breach of the peace had been committed, and was over, the constable must proceed in the same way as any other person, namely; by obtaining a warrant from a magistrate."

The American authorities establish the same rule.

In re Sarah Way, 41 Mich. 299; Commonwealth v. Carey, 12 Cush. 246. 

This court has held that a city council may lawfully authorise police officers to arrest upon view any person found in the act of violating the ordinances of the city, made for the preservation of good order and public convenience. White v. Kent, 11 Ohio St. 550.

Also that the officer in making arrest upon view is not bound to disclose his official character. Wolfe v. State, 19 Ohio St. 248. And that it is lawful to arrest, without warrant, one who is unlawfully carrying a concealed weapon, though the officer had no previous knowledge of the fact if he acted bona fide upon knowledge which induced an honest belief that the person was violating the law in this respect.
