41. Specific Facts to Be Stated.

To say that one is guilty of burglary is a true statement, if it is true, only in case certain facts exist, a breaking and entering, the dwelling-house of another, in the nighttime, with an intent to commit a felony therein. From these facts, being proved and connected with the person named as agent, the deduction follows, as matter of law, that he has committed burglary. The charge, in the form stated, is therefore a pure legal conclusion, which (if valid) must result from certain specific facts, and the validity of which cannot be tested unless such facts are known to exist or not to exist.¹ 

Having regard to the purposes of pleading generally, and in particular to the objects which an indictment is intended to attain,2 it is manifest that an accusation asserting only that a person has committed a certain crime, and not mentioning the acts and circumstances from which the guilt imputed to him results, would wholly fail to accomplish those purposes, and would be essentially inapt to the objects intended. Whence it becomes evidently necessary that the charge of an offence shall be "a statement of the facts by which it is constituted." It is, therefore, an elementary principle that a criminal pleading is insufficient if it merely propounds that a certain person has violated some law, but such a charge must set forth the facts composing the offence designated, or some other offence, enumerating specific acts of misconduct which 3

42. Completeness Requisite-Ingredients of the Crime. 

The specific facts indicated in the last preceding section as going to constitute an offence are often spoken of as the Ingredients of the Crime, being the elementary matters which collectively compose and make up the criminal conduct which an indictment purports to assert against the accused. Certain violations of the law are so simple that they may be described and charged as a single fact; thus, it is sufficient to say that the defendant assaulted one 

J. S., or committed an assault upon him, or committed an affray 2 assault and affray, and a few other instances of misbehavior, being completely stated by such compendious terms without further specification of what was done. 

But, "with rare exceptions, offences consist of more than one ingredient; and the rule is universal that every ingredient of which the offence is composed must be accurately and clearly alleged in the indictment, or the indictment will be bad, and may be quashed on motion, or the judgment may be arrested or reversed on error.

Or, as it is sometimes expressed, "It is an elementary rule of criminal pleading that every fact or circumstance which is a necessary ingredient in a prima facie case of guilt must be set out in the complaint or indictment."4

Thus, larceny is a composite crime resulting from the combination of a stealing, a taking and an asportation of another's goods, with a felonious intent. Therefore an indictment intended to make out that delinquency specifies each of these elements, alleging that the accused did feloniously steal, take and carry away certain personal property of a named owner. 

Again, in other cases, the conduct to be criminal, must involve, not only acts done by the defendant, but conditions of fact extraneous to those acts, such as knowledge on his part,5 or the presence of some other person, or

42. Offences Stated Generally. 

The requirement stated in the last preceding section admits of an exception in respect of certain violations of law which consist, not of particular acts, but of a course of conduct which is criminal.¹ 

Thus, at common law a common scold 2 and a common barrator were punishable for being what they were rather than for any single instances of scolding or barratry; wherefore in such cases the indictment charged that the defendant was of the reprehensible character specified without assigning the several occasions of misbehavior which collectively made her or him obnoxious to the law.* 

In like manner where the offence defined is a vicious habit, as street walking or night walking, it may be stated as such, without enumerating the several facts which indicate that the delinquency is habitual; and where the forbidden thing can be accomplished only by a multitude of minor activities conducing to the ultimate offence, as fitting out a ship for unlawful use, the final fact is sufficiently charged without describing the details of which it is composed. So statutes sometimes make it a crime to engage in or to carry on a certain business," or to do so with a certain intent or in a particular manner; in which cases the offender may be held to answer upon an indictment which asserts simply that he engaged in that business, or carried it on with the ill intent or in the wrong 7. 43. Essential Elements. 

Every offence is defined either by the common law or by the statute making it criminal. The facts which, by such definition, constitute guilt may be considered the essential elements of the crime; and in charging the crime, those facts must, of course, be alleged to exist. Thus, in an indictment for burglary, it is necessary to state a breaking and entering, the dwelling house of another person, in the nighttime, with intent to commit some felony therein those facts being the requisite constituents of a burglary as defined by the common law. So arson, as so defined, is a willful and malicious burning of another's house; whence it follows that in charging that crime, willfulness and malice are requisite facts to be alleged in addition to the burning.2 The statutory offence of embezzlement, as the statutes are usually drawn, consists of converting goods which have come to the possession of the offender by reason of his employment as clerk or servant or in some like character of agency; therefore, to bring a case of that nature within the statutory definition, the accusation must disclose that the defendant was in some such way employed and that the goods misappropriated were possessed by him in virtue of his employment.3 So if the definition, by common law or by statute, prescribes the presence of other things than the acts done, such as knowledge of extraneous facts,3 a certain intent or purpose, and like additional incidents of the transaction, the existence of those facts is necessary to be shown in order to bring the conduct of the accused within the purview of the criminal law relating to the delinquency asserted.5 Intent. But it is not necessary, in charging such acts to allege expressly that the actor intended to do wrong, that fact being in general sufficiently implied by showing that he did something unlawful. If facts rebutting that inference exist-such as ignorance of facts, accident and the like-those are matters of defence, which need not be rebutted by anticipation. Moreover, a criminal intent is imputed by certain adverbs, words of art (sec. 44), one or more of which are always employed to impart criminal quality to the act alleged, by importing the manner in which it was done and the mental condition of the accused: thus, in larceny the taking and asportation are said to have been done feloniously, which sufficiently asserts an intent to deprive the owner of the goods of his property therein; and in burglary the breaking and entering are described as accomplished burglariously, which negatives the possibility of accident or mistake.9 

Statutory offences are so defined by the enactments creating them as to require or not to require either a general intent to violate the law or some specific intent, as to kill or to defraud. Where such intent is included in the statutory definition, an express averment that the act was done or omitted with that intent must be made in an indictment for violating the statute, since otherwise the violation would not be complete.10 In many instances, however, statutes prohibit certain conduct without indicating whether or not any intention or other mental state must exist to make delinquency punishable: thus it is often forbidden by legislation to sell unwholesome provisions or intoxicants or narcotics, and statutes enacted in the exercise of the police power prescribe regulations concerning the details of building construction and like matters affecting the public safety and order; and such statutes quite commonly omit any mention of intent or knowledge as req-

44. Words of Art. 

As has been said,' certain adverbs and adverbial phrases are used in criminal pleading to signify the manner wherein an unlawful act was done and the mental condition of the actor. In the usus loquendi of the pleader's art these words and verbal formulas have a technically precise meaning which distinctly characterises the offence stated and develops the exact criminous quality of the conduct described. The several forms of language being severally appropriate to different degrees and forms of crime are required by the common law to be employed in charging the offences to which they are, respectively, appropriate; and so necessary are they when required that no other modes of expression, however closely synonymous or approximately equivalent, will supply the omission of the fixed phraseology. Hence such adverbs and forms of wording are called words of art, being the technical terms which alone embody, with the requisite precision and sufficiency, the ideas intended. 3 2 Thus, at common law every indictment for any degree of treason must allege that the acts constituting the crime were done traitorously; and every

In an accusation of burglary the acts specified must be asserted as done, not only feloniously, but burglariously; and in a charge of piracy the conduct must be alleged as committed piratically as well as feloniously. In murder the killing must be described as done feloniously and also with malice aforethought; and there must be added a conclusion declaring that the defendant did, of his aforesaid malice aforethought, kill and murder the decedent (sec. 38, par. 3). In charging rape the prescribed form alleges that the accused did feloniously ravish and carnally know the woman; and in robbery it must appear that the defendant did feloniously assault the owner of the property and take it by violence, or violently, from his person or in his presence. In all charges of crime involving actual breach of the peace the wrong must be described as committed with force and arms. 

Unlawfully is frequently used in charging both felonies and misdemeanors; but the word is not necessary where the crime existed at common law and is manifestly illegal. If, however, the indictment is upon a statute which includes the word in defining the offence, the act must be charged as done unlawfully.

Willfully must be used in an indictment for arson, being required by the definition of that crime, and in charging a statutory offence if the statutory definition includes willfulness.9

Some misdemeanors require particular words of allegation, as the offence or being a common scold or a common barrator, in charging which the defendant is described by those words; and in an accusation of rioting the word riot must be employed.

Collateral Facts. 1 An act may be innocent in itself but become criminal by reason of the circumstances in which it is done: to build a house is not unlawful, but if a house is so placed as to obstruct a highway, or if the construction is carried in such manner as to create a nuisance, the building of the house may be indictable. In cases of this kind,¹ where what the defendant did amounts to a breach of the law only because of concurrent conditions or of facts additional to his personal conduct, it is necessary to state such conditions or other facts in order to complete the charge of wrongdoing.2 Thus, if what was done would be lawful unless some other person were present, an indictment for doing that act must allege the presence of another person.

Sumpter was found guilty of murder in the second degree, which offence was defined by a statute quoted in the opinion below. This motion in arrest of judgment was overruled, and judgment entered upon the verdict. The judgment was affirmed.

Our statute defines murder in the second degree as follows: "The unlawful killing of a human being when perpetrated by any act imminently dangerous to another, and evincing a depraved mind regardless of human life, although without any premeditated design to effect the death of any particular individual, it shall be murder in the second degree."

U. S., 148 U. S. 197, 37 L. ed. 419, 13 S. Ct. 542. Neither is it necessary that an indictment charging murder in the second degree should allege that the act producing the death was an act imminently dangerous to another, but it is sufficient to describe the act as does the indictment here, and leaving it to the law and to the courts to say whether such act was imminently dangerous to another. We think that the courts will take judicial notice of the fact that to shoot a man with a shotgun loaded with gunpowder and leaden balls is an act imminently dangerous to the person shot from the bare statement of the act itself, and that it would be superfluous to add, after stating such act that it was imminently dangerous to the person so shot.
