2. In equity and admiralty practice the appellate jurisdiction is invoked by an appeal, which differs in function and effect from a writ of error: "An appeal is a civil law process and removes a cause entirely, subjecting the law and the facts to a review and retrial. A writ of error is a common law process, and removes for examination nothing but the law:" per Ellsworth, C. J., in Wiscart v. Dauchy, 3 

Dallas, 321, 1 L. ed. 619; quoted in U. 

S. v. Goodwin, 7 Cranch, 108, 3 L. ed. 

284. Same distinction stated in ef fect: Armsperger v. Crawford, 101 

Md. 247, 61 Atl. 413, 70 L.R.A. 497; 

Sullivan v. Haug. 82 Mich. 548, 46 N.

W. 795, 10 L.R.A. 263. The essential difference is that in equity and admiralty causes an appeal takes up all the proceedings had in the court below, including the evidence, and the appellate court is called upon to pass on the questions of fact so presented. as well as on the questions of law; whereas in a case of legal nature, the writ of error carries up only the record, which does not include the evidence or the other things occurring at the trial, so that only questions of law are presented, all uestions of fact being conclusively determined by the

whom a judgment has been pronounced in a court of first instance seeks to obtain a reversal by showing that such judgment resulted from errors committed by that court. The errors to be corrected are only such as appear upon the face of the record transmitted to the appellate tribunal. That record, as has been intimated (sec. 68, notes 11-15, ante), may consist of two elements: (1) the common law record, comprising the process, the pleadings, the verdict, the judgment, and the minutes of the court made in the course of the trial and recording the steps taken in its progress; and (2) the bill of exceptions, the statutory supplementation of the common law record," whereby are set forth such actions taken by the trial court as have been objected to and made the subjects of exceptions by the defeated party in the course of the trial or in other proceedings which are not disclosed by the common law record.

Accordingly, the plaintiff in error may, without a bill of exceptions, invoke appellate revision and correction of any defects in the pleadings which would be grounds for general demurrer and have not been aided by the verdict, and any errors in the conduct of the case which are elsewhere disclosed by the common law record and appear to have been prejudicial to the defendant. 

If exceptions to the action of the court in respect of matters not embodied in that record have been duly reserved and incorporated into a bill of exceptions, such bill becomes part of the record transmitted on the writ of error to the appellate court; and that court may be expected to reverse the judgment for any errors in point of law which are manifested by the bill of exceptions and have operated to the prejudice of the accused. jury in making their verdict, and the evidence being reproduced in a bill of exceptions only to the extent and in the mode requisite to disclose how the points of law arose: Lees v. In the common law scheme of procedure an appellate court is competent to consider only the questions of law presented by the record sent up from the court of original jurisdiction; and reversal must be had, if at all, upon a holding that error in law has intervened in the proceeding. This limitation excludes from consideration on writ of error all suggestions of wrong action in respect of matters of fact, such as a mistake of the jury in finding that certain facts do or do not exist. Accordingly, that writ does not warrant reversal of the judgment on the ground that the evidence, reported in the bill of exceptions, is not sufficient to support the verdict or that the actual facts of the case should have been found otherwise than as the jury has found them to be. And such is the law in some jurisdictions, and is held in a number of them to be the rule made necessary by certain constitutional inhibitions. 

In many States, however, the proper scope of appellate revision is defined by statutes which, to a greater or less extent, enable or require the higher court to examine matters of fact manifested by the bill of exceptions, such as the sufficiency of the evidence to warrant the findings of the jury; and in such States a judgment may be reversed and a new trial directed if the reviewing judges, 218 U. S. 245, 54 L ed. 1021, 31 S. Ct.

Appeals in Criminal Cases. In a number of jurisdictions the writ of error has been discarded in criminal cases and other actions at law, and an appeal is substituted as the mode of invoking revision of the record by an appellate court.11

The effect of the appeal in such cases, and the limitations of the appellate jurisdiction therein, are identical with those formerly obtaining when the cause was removed to the higher tribunal by writ of error, the alteration being no more than a change of name for the proceeding and a slight difference in some technical incidents of the procedure. The appeal so provided for does not, as does the appeal in equity and admiralty causes, carry up the entire case made in the court of first instance, including the testimony taken at the trial; nor is the court appealed to required or authorised to examine the evidence and pass upon questions of fact, or to take notice of other incidents of the proceeding below, otherwise than would be proper and necessary were the record brought up by writ of error, the matters mentioned being presentable on appeal (as on writ of error) only by a bill of exceptions.18 12

S. Ct. 470.]

LANNING, J.: The first assignment of error is based on the refusal of the court to grant the defendant's motion to quash the indictment. A motion to quash is ordinarily addressed to the discretion of the court, and a refusal to grant it cannot generally be assigned for error. Logan v. United States, 144 U. S. 263, 36 L. ed. 429, 12 S. Ct. 617; Durland v. United States, 161 U. S. 306, 40 L. ed. 709, 16 S. Ct. 508. 

Where the objection goes to the constitution of the jury, the old common law practice, if the ground of objection was discovered before the finding of the bill, was to challenge the jurors objected to, and, if it was discovered after such finding, to file a plea in abatement. 

That rule is generally applicable in this country. Crowley v. United States, 194

The refusal to quash could not finally determine any right of the defendant. Where an indictment is on its face manifestly defective in substance, and not in mere form, the motion to quash will usually be granted. But the motion, even in such a case is not granted ex debito justitiae. It may be overruled and the defendant be compelled to resort to his other remedies, such as demurrer, motion to direct a verdict, or motion in arrest of judgment. The first assignment of error is overruled.

POLLOCK, J.: We have treated the defendant's "motion to quash" as a demurrer, because it attacks the sufficiency of the facts set out in the indictment, and is not confined to an attack upon the validity of the indictment. If, however, it should be treated as a motion to quash in the proper sense, the overruling thereof is ordinarily not assignable as error. The indictment is sufficient, in any event, when attacked only by a motion to quash. 

In the headnote to the opinion in United States v. Rosenberg, 74 U. S. (7 

Wall.) 580, 19. L. Ed. 263, it is said: "This court cannot take cognizance,

under the Judiciary Act of 1802, of a division of opinion between the judges of the Circuit Court, upon a motion to quash an indictment.” 

In the opinion of the court, delivered by Mr. Chief Justice Chase, it is said: "The motion to quash, upon which the question now before us arose, was clearly determinable as a matter of discretion. It was preliminary in its character, and the denial of the motion could not finally decide any right of the defendant. The rule laid down by the elementary writer is, that 'a motion to quash is addressed to the sound discretion of the court, and if refused, is not a proper subject of exception." 779 

In Durland v. United States, 161 U. S. 306, 40 L. ed. 709, 16 S. Ct. 508, 511, the great lawyer, Mr. Justice Brewer, in delivering the opinion for the court, said: "These objections were raised by a motion to quash the indictment, but such a motion is ordinarily addressed to the discretion of the court, and a refusal to quash is not, generally, assignable for error. Logan v. United 

States, 144 U. S. 263-282, 36 L. ed. 429, 12 S. Ct. 617." 

In Endleman v. United States (C. C. A.) 86 F. 456, 458, it is said: "The objections raised by the motion to quash the indictment may be dismissed with the observation that a motion to quash an indictment is ordinarily addressed to the discretion of the court, and therefore a refusal to quash cannot generally be assigned as error." Citing U. S. v. Rosenberg, 7 Wall. 580, 19 L. ed. 263; U. S. v. Hamilton, 109 U. S. 63, 27 L. ed. 857, 3 S. Ct. 9; Logan v. 

U. S., 144 U. S. 263, 36 L ed. 429, 12 S. Ct. 617. In 22 Cyc. 413, it is said: "A motion to quash an indictment is ordinarily addressed to the discretion of the court, the accused not being entitled to demand a quashal as a matter of right. A refusal to grant the motion is for this reason not usually assignable error."

The above text is well supported by authorities cited. 

State v. Jellison, 104 Me. 281, 71 Atl. 716. Supreme Judicial Court of Maine. 1908. 

In a municipal court Jellison was tried and acquitted upon a charge of assault and battery alleged as committed on Henry N. 

Pringle. Afterward, in a superior court, an indictment was brought against Jellison charging him with the statutory offence of unlawful assembly and riot, and alleging that he, with several other persons, did unlawfully and tumultuously assemble to make an assault upon Henry N. Pringle and did assault and beat Pringle. Jellison pleaded to the indictment that he had been acquitted of assault and battery upon Pringle, the plea averring that the assault and battery and the offence charged in the indictment were one and the same offence. To this plea the State demurred, and the demurrer was sustained. To this action of the trial court the defendant excepted. The exception was overruled by the Supreme Judicial Court, which thereupon proceeded to enter final judgment against the defendant, without affording him opportunity to plead over to the merits of the case. 

EMERY, C. J.: The demurrer, of course, did not admit the correctness of any statements or conclusions of law made in the plea. 

Hence, though it admits that the acts of the defendant were the same in both cases, it does not admit that the offences charged are

one and the same offense. Whether they are the same or different offences is question of law now to be determined by the court. . . . 

It is to be noted that the Constitution does not prohibit a second jeopardy for the same act, or group of acts, but only "for the same offense." Dec. of Rights, art. 1, § 8. The acts and the offense they constitute are different things, and the same acts may constitute more than one offense, and also different offenses, subjecting the actor to as many punishments as the offenses his acts constitute. 

Thus a person by the same acts, or group of acts, may violate the statute against selling liquors; also the statute against being a common seller of intoxicating liquors; also that against keeping a drinking house and tippling shop; and also that against maintaining a common nuisance. If he be charged and convicted, or acquitted, of the violation of one of these statutes, he has been put in jeopardy only for that one offense, and not for the offense of violating any of the other statutes. State v. Coombs, 32 Me. 529; State v. Maher, 35 Me. 225; State v. Inness, 53 Me. 536. In the opinion of the court in this last case are cited many instances where it was held that a person may be punished more than once for the same act where the act constitutes more than one offense. We refer the reader to that opinion for the cases. 79 The offense of assault and battery and the offense of unlawful assembly or riot are different offenses. Neither included the other. 

A person may commit either without committing the other. Nevertheless the same acts may sometimes constitute both offenses; but, when they do, the offenses are still different though the acts are the same, and the perpetrator of the acts may be punished twice, once for each offense. State v. Inness, 53 Me. 536, at page 537;

Hurd v. State, 2 Root (Conn.) 186; U. S. v. Peaco, Fed. Cas. No. 

16,018; Freeland v. People, 16 Ill. 380. We are aware that in some states the courts hold otherwise, but we think the above is the law of this state. It follows that the exceptions must be overruled. 

In the case of State v. Inness, 53 Mc. 536, where the court overruled the exceptions to sustaining a demurrer to a plea of former jeopardy, final judgment was ordered for the state after full consideration of the question whether the judgment should be final or only respondeas ouster. The decision was based on Rev. St. 1857, c. 77, § 28, now Rev. St. 1903, c. 79, § 56. "When a dilatory plea is overruled and exceptions taken, the court shall proceed and close the trial, and the action shall then be continued and marked law,'" ctc. The defendant's plea of former jeopardy was a dilatory plea, since, if overruled, the judgment, but for the statute cited, would be simply respondeas ouster. He pleaded his dilatory plea alone, without obtaining leave to plead double, and, his plea having been adjudged insufficient, he excepted, and, without obtaining leave to plead over if his exceptions should be overruled, he brought them

directly to the law court before the trial was closed. Under the statute it must be held that by taking the course he did he waived whatever right he may have had to plead over when his dilatory plea was overruled, and that, having thus elected to abide by that plea, he must fall with it. State v. Inness, 53 Me. 536; Furbish v. Robertson, 67 Me. 35, page 38; Smith v. Hunt, 91 Me. 572, 40 

Atl. 698.

Wilburn v. State, 21 Ark. 198. Supreme Court of Arkansas. 1860. 

To an indictment charging Wilburn with the illegal sale of spirituous liquors, he pleaded in abatement certain facts which, if proven, would render the selection of the grand jury irregular. A demurrer to the plea was sustained, whereupon the court gave final judgment of guilty against the accused and imposed a fine. The judgment was reversed. 

COMPTON, J.: The courts are strict in discountenancing irregularities in the mode of selecting and empanelling grand jurors, and the decided weight of American authority is that objection may be taken to the irregularity by plea in abatement: Leathers v. State, 26 Miss. 33; State v. Symonds, 36 Me. 128; 

State v. Newer, 7 Blackford, 307.

In framing pleas of this character, it is said the greatest accuracy and precision are required, and that they should be certain to every intent. Under our system, there are two modes by which a grand jury may be lawfully selected. One is, where they are selected pursuant to the provisions of the statute; and the other is, where the Circuit Court causes them to be selected, in the exercise of its inherent constitutional power as held by the court in 

Straughan v. The State, 16 Ark. 37. The plea sufficiently negatives a selection in either mode.

According to this view, the plea was good, and the court erred in sustaining the demurrer.

The court erred also, in rendering final judgment. On sustaining the demurrer, the judgment should have been that the defendant answer over; and if he declined to do so, the court should have directed the plea of not guilty to be entered for him, and that the cause proceed to trial, as decided in Buzzard v. The State, 20 Ark. 106.

In misdemeanors, where the defendant pleads matter in abatement, and upon an issue to the plea, the finding is against him, he is not allowed to plead over, and the judgment is final, as in Guess v. The State, 1 Eng. 147; 

McCuen v. The State, 19 Ark. 630; but not so, where a demurrer is sustained to the plea and this is the distinction between the cases last cited and 

Buzzard v. The State, supra. 

Welch v. State, 68 Miss. 341, 8 So. 673. Supreme Court of 

Mississippi. 1891.

Welch, the appellant, was indicted for the crime of abduction. 

To the indictment Welch pleaded in abatement that one J. S. Sexton, an attorney at law engaged in the prosecution of the case, was permitted to go before the grand jury when they were considering the matter of finding an indictment against him. To this plea the state replied that said Sexton went before the grand jury in obedience to a summons from that body. Welch rejoined that said Sexton had procured himself to be summoned as a witness, and had argued before the grand jury that it should find an indictment.

The state demurred to the rejoinder. The demurrer was sustained, and the trial resulted in a verdict and judgment against Welch, from which he appealed.

CAMPBELL, J. If it be true that an attorney for the prosecution of Welch procured himself to be summoned as a witness to appear before the grand jury, and by this means was introduced into their room, and addressed the grand jury, urging the finding of an indictment in this matter, the indictment should be quashed. Illegal or insufficient evidence before the grand jury will not be inquired into, but the array may be excepted to for fraud; and improper influences to secure an indictment may be inquired into, and should be, when properly alleged. In vain the constitution protects against being proceeded against criminally, by information, for an indictable offense, except in cases mentioned, if grand juries are to be swayed by malice or prejudice, or subjected to other influences than those recognized by law as legitimate and proper to guide them in their secret inquest. "The recognition of such a mode of reaching grand juries [as was alleged in this case] would introduce a flood of evils disastrous to the purity of the administration of criminal justice, and subversive of all public confidence in the action of these bodies." It is true that one indicted is to be tried by his peers, and, if falsely accused, may expect a deliverance; but he is entitled to attack the prosecution in limine, where it is procured by means unknown to and unsanctioned by law. The demurrer to the rejoinder should have been overruled. Reversed, demurrer overruled, and cause remanded. 

State v. McNay, 100 Md. 622, 60 Atl. 273. Court of Appeals, Maryland. 1905.

To an indictment charging McNay with unlawfully selling intoxicating liquor, he put in a plea in abatement alleging three facts, that the grand jury which returned the indictment was not composed of 23 lawful jurors, that the grand jurors were not selected in accordance with the statutory prescription on that subject, and that the statute under which the grand jury had been drawn was unconstitutional. To this plea the State filed a general demurrer, upon the argument of which it was contended that the plea was bad for duplicity. The demurrer was overruled by the trial court and judgment given for the defendant. This judgment was reversed upon an appeal taken by the State. The particular irregularity in selecting the grand jurors, which was alleged by the plea, was that the jury commissioners, who were charged with the duty of selecting, had accepted lists of names voluntarily made up by persons not commissioners, and that the commissioners had put upon the panel some persons so suggested, some of such nominees being incompetent and disqualified to officiate as grand jurors. The plea did not allege that

the names furnished to the commissioners were not upon the tax lists and poll-books, or that the commissioners did not make due inquiry and exercise independent judgment in selecting the persons to be placed upon the panel. 

PEARSE, J.: The authorities agree that all pleadings are double which contain several answers, whatever the class or quality of the answer, whether in abatement or in bar. Stephen on Pleading, p. 258; Gould on Pleading, c. 8, § 1; 7 Enc. Pl. and Pr. 238. Mr. Bishop, in his new Crim. Proc. vol. 1, § 432, states the rule thus: "Alike in criminal and civil proceedings, duplicity consists in alleging for one single purpose or object two or more distinct grounds of complaint or defense when one alone would be effectual in law." 

Mr. Stephen, on page 242 (Tyler's Ed.), says that the meaning of this rule with respect to the declaration (or indictment) is "that it must not, in support of a single demand (or charge), allege several distinct matters made, by any one of which that demand (or charge) is sufficiently supported; and with respect to the subsequent pleadings the meaning is that none of them is to contain several distinct answers to that which preceded it, and the reason of the rule in each case is that such pleading tends to several issues in respect of a single claim." And again, on pages 245 and 246, he says that, although a plea may make distinct answers to such parts of a declaration as relate to different matters of claim or complaint, "none of the matters so alleged in a plea in abatement must be such as would alone be a sufficient answer to the whole," and he gives the following illustration: "The defendant pleaded in disability of the person of the plaintiff ten different outlawries adjudged against him, and it was held that the plea was ill for duplicity, because the plaintiff was disabled as well by one outlawry as by the whole ten." So here the grand jury would be as effectually shown to be an unlawfully constituted body by proof of any one of the matters pleaded, as of all, assuming all of these matters to be valid objections to its organization. For this reason we think this plea is bad for duplicity. At common law it would seem to be clear that demurrer is a proper mode of taking advantage of this defect. 1 Bishop's New Crim. Proc. § 442. Mr. Poe, in section 738 of his work on Pleading, calls attention to the fact that the act of 1888 omitted from section 10 of article 75 the words, "and that no one plea contain distinct matters of defense or reply," which were previously contained therein, and adds that since that act duplicity is no longer the subject of demurrer in this state. But in Stearns v. State, 81 Md. 341, 32 Atl. 282 (decided in 1895), an information for violation of the gambling act was held bad for duplicity, and we therefore hold this demurer should have been sustained. Moreover, this plea is lacking in certainty. In Bishop's New Crim. Proc. § 327, the author, speaking of pleas in abatement, says: "This superlative certainty requires the utmost fullness and particularity of statement, as well as the highest attainable accuracy and precision, leaving on the one hand nothing to be supplied by intendment or construction, and on the other no supposable special answer not obviated." And in State v. Scarborough, 55

Md. 350, it is said: "Every dilatory plea must be pleaded with strictness, and be certain to every intent; and it is consequently essential that the facts should be stated out of which the defense arises, or a negation of the facts presumed from the existence of a record." To meet these exacting requirements so clearly stated by Mr. Bishop and so emphasized by this court in the Scarborough Case, this plea should have stated in affirmative language that the names furnished by other persons were voluntarily suggested by them without inquiry or request from the jury commissioners, and were not independently selected and approved by them after examination, and were not names upon the tax lists or pollbooks; thus negativing of the supposable special answers that their names were upon the proper lists, and were furnished by request of the commissioners. The second objection therefore cannot avail to invalidate the grand jury.

McCuen v. State, 19 Ark. 630. Supreme Court of Arkansas. 1858.

McCuen being charged with the misdemeanor of unlawfully selling ardent spirits, he put in a demurrer to the indictment. The court overruled the demurrer and at once rendered final judgment against the defendant, imposing a fine of $50. This judgment was affirmed. 

ENGLISH, C. J.: By the comomn law the judgment of the court upon demurrer to an indictment for felony, is respondeat ouster; but if the defendant demur to an indictment for a misdemeanor, and fail on the argument, he shall not have judgment to answer over, but the decision will operate as a conviction-the judgment is final. 8 East 112; Haw. b. 2 e. 31; 

1 Chitty Cr. L. 441; Wharton Cr. L. 186, (2d Ed.).

The current of decisions in this country is that on overruling a demurrer to an indictment for misdemeanor, the Court may, in its discretion, permit the defendant to plead over, but he cannot claim it as a matter of right. The 

People v. Taylor, 3 Denio 98; Evans v. Commonwealth, 3 Metcalf 453; Burnett v. The State, 2 Yerger 472; State v. Shaw et al., 8 Humph. R. 32; State v. Wilkins, 17 Vermont 152; Wickwire v. The State, 19 Conn. 477. 

Rex v. Gibson, 8 East, 107, 103 Eng. Reprint, 284. King's Bench. 1806.

Gibson was indicted by the name of Benjamin Gibson for an assault. He pleaded in abatement that his name was not Benjamin, but Benoni. A replication was put in traversing the name alleged by the plea, and upon trial of the issue so made there was a verdict finding the plea untrue. Thereupon 

Gibson obtained a rule requiring the prosecutor to show cause why the defendant should not be at liberty to plead not guilty to the indictment. The rule was discharged and final judgment rendered against the defendant. 

LORD ELLENBOROUGH, C. J.: The general principle of the common law is against pleading over after a plea in abatement found against the defendant; but there are several privileged cases, which are admitted by way of exception, and one of them is in case of felony, in favorem vitae, and that extends to felony generally; because at common law the judgment is of death, though clergy may be demandable. Only one instance has been mentioned of the same privilege allowed in a case of misdemeanor, and that is the precedent referred to in Tremaine, which may have passed in the mere exercise of a discretionary power by the Court, on account of the magnitude of the punishment for striking another in the King's palace, being no less than the loss of the offender's hand: But at any rate, the general point does not appear to have been presented to the notice of the Court in judicial debate; but it is cited merely from an entry in a book of entries. On the other hand, the exception in case of felony in favorem vitae, is expressly recognised by Lord Hale, who derives it from the case in the year books; and it is since adopted by Hawkins, though of less authority than Lord Hale, and stands also upon the case in Popham's Reports. When therefore the books agree in considering felony as an excepted case in favorem vitae, they in effect exclude all other cases not also excepted: and if persons indicted for misdemeanors had been considered as entitled to the same privilege of pleading double, there must have been many instances of their having availed themselves of it to be met with in the books, many more probably than in cases of felony. 

LAWRENCE, J. Referred to 2 Hawk. ch. 31, s. 6 & 7. which says, that "Howsoever the law may stand in relation to a general demurrer concluding in bar of an appeal or indictment, as in common demurrers in civil actions, &c. which admits the fact, &c.; it hath been adjudged, that if an appellee demur in law to an appeal by reason of the insufficiency of the declaration, or generally demur to the declaration, with a conclusion, et petit judicium de narra-

OBJECTIONS TO THE INDIOTMENT 

523 tione illa, et quod narratio illa cassetur, &c.; such demurrer shall not conclude him from pleading over to the felony, either at the same time with the demurrer, or after it shall be adjudged against him. But it seems, that in criminal cases, not capital, if the defendant demur to an indictment, &c., whether in abatement or otherwise, the Court will not give judgment against him to answer over, but final judgment." 

People v. McKenna, 81 Cal. 158, 22 Pac. 488. Supreme Court of California. 1889.

PATERSON, J.: The defendant was tried and convicted on an information which charged that "on or about the 15th day of July, 1888, at the county of San Luis Obispo, state of California, [the defendant,] did unlawfully, knowingly, and designedly, by false and fraudulent representations and pretenses, defraud one David Taylor of personal property to-wit, twenty hogs, of the value of two hundred and three and forty one-hundredths dollars in lawful money of the United States, the personal property of the said David 

Taylor, contrary to the form, force," etc.

The most important question in the case is whether the facts stated are sufficient to support a conviction. There was no demurrer to the complaint, but there was a motion in arrest of judgment, and a motion for a new trial. It is claimed on behalf of the respondent that the information is sufficient, in the absence of a demurrer; that, if the defendant had desired the information to be made more specific, he should have demurred on the ground that it did not substantially conform to the requirements of sections 950-952 of the Penal Code. If, however, the facts stated in the information do not constitute a public offense, the objection to its sufficiency may be made at any time. In civil cases the rule is, as stated by Mr. Justice Temple, that the plaintiff is not required "to allege with minuteness all the particulars and circumstances which constitute the evidence of the alleged fraud, but he must make the charge with sufficient distinctness to enable his adversary to come prepared with his evidence upon the general questions of fraud, which will be raised." Capuro v. Insurance Co., 39 Cal. 125. It matters not that no objection is made by demurrer. Objection may be made at any time, because it goes to the substance of the complaint or indictment.

The question whether a thing has been done fraudulently is a matter of law, and an allegation of fraud in general terms presents no issuable facts. Meeker v. Harris, 19 Cal. 289, 290; Triscony v. Orr, 49 Cal. 617; Bank v. Hynes, 50 Cal. 202. Where no facts are averred, no facts are admitted. Payne v. Elliot, 54 Cal. 343; 

Johnson v. Kirby, 65 Cal. 487, 4 Pac. Rep. 458. It is said by Mr.

Bishop that "to charge simply in the statutory words that the thing was obtained by 'false pretenses' is not adequate. What the particular pretenses were must be stated, both as notice to the defend- 1

ant of what he has to answer to, and as enabling the court to discern their indictable quality. A pretense, as set out, must be adequate in law. For example, it must be of an existing fact; not a promise. And it must be stated in a form direct; not argumentative.

Therefore an allegation which did not distinguish clearly whether it was promise or fact was adjudged ill." 2 Bish. Crim. Proc. §§ 165, 166. Mr. Wharton says an information charging simply that the defendant obtained goods by false pretenses "would be scouted out of court." 1 Whart. Crim. Law, § 192. As said in 

U. S. v. Watkins, 3 Cranch, C. C. 441: "Fraud is an inference of law from certain facts, and the indictment must aver all the facts which constitute the fraud. 

To aver that an act was fraudulently done is therefore to aver a matter of law, and not a matter of fact." It is a sound principle that an indictment charging fraud of any kind should aver with particularity the facts relied upon to show fraud. Many of the niceties and technicalities which existed under former methods of pleading are not allowed to prevail under the provisions of our Code; but the rule still exists that an indictment must be certain and clear as to "the particular circumstances of the offense charged, when they are necessary to constitute a complete offense." Pen. Code, § 952, subd. 3. 

Pen. Code, § 952, subd. 3. It is true that, as a general rule, an indictment is sufficient if it describes the offense in the words of the statute; but, as said by Mr. Justice Harlan in 

U. S. v. Simmons, 96 U. S. 360, 24 L. ed. 819: "To this general rule there is the qualification, fundamental in the law of criminal procedure, that the accused must be apprised by the indictment with reasonable certainty of the nature of the accusation against him, to the end that he may prepare his defense, and plead the judgment as a bar to any subsequent prosecution for the same offense." The conviction under the information before us, and the judgment entered thereon, could not be safely or successfully pleaded in bar of a second prosecution for the same offense. It is alleged simply that the defendant unlawfully, knowingly, and designedly, by false and fraudulent representations and pretenses, defrauded Taylor of his personal property. The particular fraud is in no way identified. 

In our opinion, the allegations of the information are not sufficient to apprise the defendant with that certainty which the law requires of the nature of the accusation against him, to enable him to prepare a defense, or to plead the judgment as a bar to any subsequent prosecution for the same offense, and therefore that the motion in arrest of judgment should have been granted, and that the information ought to have been dismissed. U. S. v. Goggin, 9 Biss. 269, 1 Fed. Rep. 49.

A distinction is made between pleadings inartificially drawn, where there is an attempt to plead the facts, and those entirely

wanting in facts. In People v. Donaldson, 70 Cal. 116, 11 Pac.

Rep. 681, relied upon by respondent, the indictment charged that the defendant obtained the property under false pretenses, "in that he did willfully, unlawfully, knowingly, and designedly obtain from one J. P. Spence certain hogs belonging to him, and in his possession, by falsely pretending to Spence that he (the defendant) had in the Commercial & Savings Bank of San Jose the sum of $196.70, and did, with intent to cheat and defraud said Spence, make, execute, sign, and deliver to him a check upon that bank for such amount. 

The indictment further alleged that Spence was induced to part with his property by reason of such representation, and that the defendant knew at the time that he had no money or credit in the bank, and had no reason to believe that the check would be honored or paid." The difference between that case and the one before us is made plain by comparing the allegations of the indictment with those of the information herein.

The judgment is reversed, with directions to the court below to dismiss the information. 

Herron v. State, 118 Miss. 420, 79 So. 289. Supreme Court of 

Mississippi. 1918.

Herron was convicted upon an indictment reading thus: "The grand jurors, &c., upon their oaths present that one Joe Herron, late of the county aforesaid, on the 1st day of April, A. D., 1918, with force and arms, in the county aforesaid, and within the jurisdiction of this court then and there did unlawfully and feloniously obtain from Jones Smokehouse, a corporation, the sum of twenty-five ($25.00) dollars, lawful money of the United States, by means of giving to the said Jones Smokehouse a check drawn on the First National Bank of Birmingham, Alabama, he, the said Joe Herron, knowing at the time of drawing said check, and uttering and delivering the same, that he had not sufficient funds with the said First National Bank of Birmingham, Alabama, to pay said check upon its presentation, and that said check was presented by said payee within thirty days after the drawing of said check, contrary to the statutes in such case, made and provided, and against the peace and dignity of the state of Mississippi. 

Jas. D. Thames, District Attorney.

SMITH, C. J.: The indictment upon which appellant was tried, which the reporter will set out, is fatally defective, in that it contains no allegation that appellant intended to defraud Jones Smokehouse, an intent to defraud being an essential element of the crime. defined by chapter 120 of the Laws of 1916 (section 897, Hemingway's Code), upon which the indictment is predicated. 

Since the omitted allegation goes to the very essence of the of fense attempted to be charged the omission thereof was not waived by appellant's failure to demur thereto. Section 1426, Code of 

1906; section 1182, Hemingway's Code; Cook v. State, 72 Miss. 

517, 17 South. 228; Taylor v. State, 74 Miss. 544, 21 South. 129. 

Reversed and remanded.

State v. Keena, 63 Conn. 329, 28 Atl. 522. Supreme Court of 

Errors, Connecticut. 1893.

Keena was convicted upon an information charging that he did willfully and maliciously burn a certain dwelling-house. His motion in arrest of judgment was overruled and upon the verdict was entered a judgment, which was reversed. 

ANDREWS, C. J.: Every information for a criminal offence must set forth all the essential ingredients of the crime charged with reasonable certainty. If it fails to do this, it is bad on demurrer, or on a motion to arrest the judgment. State v. Costello, 62 Conn. 128, 25 Atl. 477. The essential ingredients of the crime of arson are, the voluntary and malicious burning of an occupied dwelling house, and that the house be the house of another than the accused. 2 Swift, Dig. side p. 304; 3 Co. Inst. 66. From these clements it appears that arson is an offense against the security of a dwelling house as such, and not against the building as property. 

It has regard to the occupation instead of the ownership; or rather, in the contemplation of this offense, the occupier is the owner. State v. Toole, 29 Conn. 342; State v. McGowan, 20 Conn. 245, 246;

Snyder v. People, 26 Mich. 106. And so essential is it to the idea of arson that the house burned be the house of another, that one does not commit this crime by burning the house occupied by himself. State v. Lyon, 12 Conn. 487; State v. Fish, 27 N. J. Law, 323; Breeme's Case, 2 East, P. C. 1026; Sullivan v. State, 5 Stew. & P. 175; Bloss v. Tobey, 2 Pick. 320, 325.

Counsel for the accused urge that the present information is bad because it does not give the name of any occupier of the house burned. 

They expend the principal force of their argument in seeking to show that, as there is no name of an occupier given, it does not appear that the house was an occupied one. Whether or not they are correct in that argument, we have no occasion to decide. For another reason, we think the omission to state the name of the occupier of the house renders the information fatally defective. It does not appear that the house burned was the house of another than the accused. In this particular, the name of the occupier is a necessary averment.

Either the name of the occupier must be stated, or there must be other averments from which it is made to appear that the house burned is the house of another person. In this information there are no such averments. Without them, it is clearly bad, because it does not charge the crime of arson. And it is a defect which is not cured by the verdict. "It is a general rule of pleading at common law-and upon a question of pleading at common law there is no distinction between civil and criminal casesthat where an averment which is necessary for the support of the pleadings is imperfectly stated, and the verdict on an issue involving that averment is found, if it appears to the court after verdict

that the verdict could not have been found on this issue without proof of this averment, there, after verdict, the defective averment which might have been bad on demurrer is cured by the verdict." 

Heyman v. Queen, 8 Q. B. 102. "The expression 'cured by verdict' signifies that the court will after a verdict presume that the particular thing omitted or defectively stated in the pleadings was duly proved at the trial. And such intendment must arise, not merely from the verdict, but from the united effect of the verdict and the issue upon which the verdict was given. And the particular thing which is presumed to have been proved must always be such as can be implied from the allegations of the record by fair and reasonable intendment." Jackson v. Pesked, 1 Maule & S. 234.

In overruling the motion in arrest of judgment, the superior court erred, and the judgment is reversed. 

Wilson v. United States, 275 Fed. 307. United States Circuit

Court of Appeals, Second Circuit. 1921. 

[Writ of certiorari denied in 257 U. S. 649, 66 L. ed. 416, 42 

S. Ct. 57.]

ROGERS, J.: In this case the defendants went to trial without making any objection to the indictment. There was no motion to quash, no demurrer, no application for a bill of particulars. As they went to trial without any objection, now that they have been convicted they cannot come into this court to raise objections which must have been met at the trial. If the defects existed, and we do not think they did, they are defects which under the rule were cured by verdict. It is the rule in criminal, as it is in civil cases, that where an averment necessary to support a particular part of an indictment has been imperfectly stated, the defect is cured by the verdict if it appears to the court that unless the averment were true the verdict could not be sustained. Heymann v. Reg., L. R. 

8 Q. B. 102, 12 Cox, C. C. 383; Reg. v. Stroulger, 17 Q. B. Div. 

327, 16 Cox, C. C. 85; State v. Ryan, 68 Conn. 512, 37 Atl. 377; 

State v. Freeman, 63 Vt. 496, 22 Atl. 621. The matters said to be indefinitely set forth could not have been proved as alleged unless the government produced all the evidence necessary to support the most careful pleadings. 

Regina v. Bowen, 13 Q. B. 790, 116 Eng. Reprint, 1465.

Queen's Bench. 1849. 

The Stat. 7 & 8 Geo. 4, ch. 29, sec. 53, enacted "That if any person shall by any false pretence obtain from any other person any chattel, money or valuable security, with intent to cheat or defraud any person of the same, every such person shall be guilty of a misdemeanor." Upon this statute an indictment was drawn charging

that Bowen had obtained money from certain named persons by means of certain false representations, which were set forth and alleged to be false. There was, however, no averment that Bowen knew the representations to be untrue, the indictment following the words of the statute, which did not specify knowledge of the falsity as an element of the offence. Bowen was found guilty and moved in arrest of judgment on the ground that there was no scienter in the indictment. The motion was denied. 

LORD DENMAN, C. J.: It appears to me that this count is sufficient. It contains a description of the offence with all the ingredients that are mentioned in the statute creating it. I know it is said that a description containing all these is not in every case sufficient; but if we can see that the description contains all the ingredients necessary to constitute the offence, the count is surely supported. The great difficulty arises from the decision in Regina v. Henderson [2 Mov. C. C. 192]. That case, however, was not fully argued, and there appears to have been an oversight, as no reference was made to the language of the last statute. 

That case, too, was decided on demurrer; in the present the objection is taken after verdict.

WIGHTMAN, J.: Undoubtedly Regina v. Henderson is an au thority that, on demurrer, the want of scienter is an objection to an indictment for false pretences. But many objections fatal on demurrer are not available in arrest of judgment, as in that stage of the case it is considered that everything put in issue was proved on the trial. And the indictment here follows the very words of the statute creating the offence, which does not use the terms "knowingly" or "designedly:" and Stat. 7 Geo. 4, ch. 64, sec. 21, says that a count shall after verdict be sufficient if it describes the offence in the words of the statute. If the count show a crime within the terms of the statute, though defectively, so as to be bad on demurrer, it is good after verdict. Regina v. Waters, 1 Denn. C. C. 

356, goes on that distinction. Here I think the count does show a crime within the meaning of the statute, though if Regina v. 

Henderson was well decided, it shows it defectively. Such knowledge as was necessary to constitute the crime must, I think, on this indictment be taken to have been proved at the trial, as the jury have found a verdict of guilty. 

Hagner v. United States, 285 U. S. 427, 76 L. ed. 861, 52 S. 

Ct. 417. Supreme Court of the United States. 1932.

Two persons named Hagner were convicted in the District of Columbia upon an indictment, set forth in the opinion, charging violation of section 215 of the Criminal Code of the United States, which makes it an offence to employ the Post Office establishment

to execute any scheme or artifice to defraud. The conviction was affirmed by the Court of Appeals of the District, 60 App. D. C. 

335, 54 Fed. (2d) 446, and on a writ of certiorari was again affirmed, though upon a ground different from that adopted by the 

Court of Appeals. 

SUTHERLAND, J.: The indictment charges that the petitioners devised and intended to devise a scheme and artifice to defraud the Merchants' Transfer & Storage Company out of its money and property in manner and form set forth; and that "for the purpose of executing said scheme and artifice, on, to wit, April 19, 1927, did place and cause to be placed in the Post Office at the City of Scranton, in the State of Pennsylvania, to be sent and delivered by the Post Office establishment of the United States of America, to the addressee thereof, three certain accounts enclosed in a certain envelope addressed to Merchants' Transfer and Storage Company, 920 

E Street, N. W., Washington, D. C." ..

The contention is that the indictment charges no offense committed in the District of Columbia, but only an offense committed in Pennsylvania; and, assuming this to be true, that the Supreme 

Court of the District of Columbia was without jurisdiction. Undoubtedly, the indictment is adequate to charge an offense committed in Pennsylvania; but the question first to be considered is whether, upon this record and upon a motion in arrest of judgment, the indictment may be sustained as also sufficient to charge an offense committed within the District of Columbia. The record brought here does not contain the evidence or any of the trial proceedings. 

We have before us only the indictment, the fact that petitioners were arraigned, entered pleas, were convicted and sentenced, the motion in arrest of judgment, and the order of the court overruling it, together with the formal docket entries relating thereto. 

The defect said to exist is that the indictment fails to allege specifically that petitioners did "cause [the letter] to be delivered by mail according to the direction thereon." Obviously, in this particular, the indictment does not precisely follow the terms of the statute, but it does allege that the letter was deposited in a post office so addressed as to constitute a direction for its delivery to the addressee at a particular place in the District of Columbia. The rule is well settled that proof that a letter properly directed was placed in a post office creates a presumption that it reached its destination in usual time and was actually received by the person to whom it was addressed. Rosenthal v. Walker, 111 U. S. 185, 193, 28 L. ed. 395, 4 S. Ct. 382. And the fact that receipt of the letter subjects the person sending it to a penalty does not alter the rule. 

Id., page 194 of 111 U. S., 28 L. ed. 398, 4 S. Ct. 382. If the indictment had alleged actual delivery of the letter in question, the case for the government in this particular would have been made 

[Cases in Crim. Proc.]-34

out by proof that the letter thus directed had been placed in the post office for transmission. The burden then would have been cast upon petitioners to show the contrary.

While, therefore, the indictment does not in set terms allege delivery of the letter, a presumption to that effect results from the facts which are alleged. In Ball v. United States, 140 U. S. 118, 133, 136, 35 L. ed. 377, 11 S. Ct. 761, it was held that an indictment for murder which fails to allege the time of the death is fatally defective, since to constitute murder it is necessary that death shall occur within a year and a day from the time of the fatal stroke. 

But it appearing that the indictment then under consideration had been returned less than a year from the day of the assault, the court did not consider the objection fatal to the indictment in this particular, notwithstanding the absence of an allegation of the time of death.

The rigor of old common-law rules of criminal pleading has yielded, in modern practice, to the general principle that formal defects, not prejudicial, will be disregarded. The true test of the sufficiency of an indictment is not whether it could have been made more definite and certain, but whether it contains the elements of the offense. intended to be charged, "and sufficiently apprises the defendant of what he must be prepared to meet, and, in case any other proceedings are taken against him for a similar offense, whether the record shows with accuracy to what extent he may plead a former acquittal or conviction." Cochran and Sayre v. United States, 157 U. S. 286, 290, 39 L. ed. 704, 15 S. Ct. 628, 630; Rosen v. United States, 161 

U. S. 29, 34, 40 L. ed. 606, 16 S. Ct. 434, 480. 

Section 1025, Revised Statutes (U. S. C., title 18, § 556 [18 USCA § 556]) provides: 

"No indictment found and presented by a grand jury in any district or other court of the United States shall be deemed insufficient, nor shall the trial, judgment, or other proceeding thereon be affected by reason of any defect or imperfection in matter of form only, which shall not tend to the prejudice of the defendant." 

This section was enacted to the end that, while the accused must be afforded full protection, the guilty shall not escape through mere imperfections of pleading. We refer to a few of the many cases where the provision has been applied. 

In Grandi v. United States (C. C. A.) 262 F. 123, 124, the indictment charged the defendant with the receipt and possession of goods knowing they had been stolen from part of a shipment in interstate commerce, but failed to charge that the goods were in fact so stolen. A motion to quash had been denied, on the ground that the defendant could not have been misled to his prejudice. The court said: "The charge that defendant knew the goods to have 

[Cases in Crim. Proc.]

been stolen naturally implies that the goods had been in fact stolen. 

The verdict should not be reversed on account of a defect so obviously technical and unsubstantial." An indictment under the Espionage Act (40 Stat. 217), which denounces certain acts when the 

United States is at war, has been upheld, notwithstanding a failure to allege that when the acts were committed the United States was at war, on the ground that the courts would take judicial notice of that fact. Stephens v. United States (C. C. A.) 261 F. 590; Bouldin v. United States (C. C. A.) 261 F. 674. An indictment for seditious conspiracy under section 6 of the Criminal Code (18 USCA $6) must charge that the conspiracy involved an intent to use force; but where the overt act was alleged, with the intent of engaging in armed hostility against the United States by attacking with force and arms, the original intent was necessarily implied and the indictment was sustained, notwithstanding the lack of the specific allegation, since otherwise effect, fatal to the indictment, would be given to a mere imperfection in matter of form, not tending to the prejudice of the defendant. Phipps v. United States (C. C. A.) 

251 F. 879, 880. Omission from an indictment, drawn under the section of the Criminal Code now under consideration, of a specific allegation that the letter was "to be sent or delivered by the post office establishment," was not considered prejudicial, where the indictment sufficiently alleged that the letter was placed in the post office properly addressed. Olsen v. United States (C. C. A.) 287 

F. 85, 90. See, also, Cohen v. United States (C. C. A.) 294 F. 

488, 490; Gay v. United States (C. C. A.) 12 F. (2d) 433, 434; 

Musey v. United States (C. C. A.) 37 F. (2d) 673, 674.

It, of course, is not the intent of section 1025 to dispense with the rule which requires that the essential elements of an offense must be alleged; but it authorizes the courts to disregard merely loose or inartificial forms of averment. Upon a proceeding after verdict at least, no prejudice being shown, it is enough that the necessary facts appear in any form, or by fair construction can be found within the terms of the indictment.

In the absence of the evidence and the charge of the court, we are free to assume that every essential element of the offense was sufficiently proved, and that the question as to the delivery of the letter was submitted under appropriate instructions to the jury. The contrary of neither of these propositions is asserted. The indictment in the particular complained of is loosely and inartificially drawn and is not to be commended, but, upon the record before us, and without deciding that the indictment would not have been open to some form of challenge at an earlier stage of the case, we are of opinion that after verdict it is not vulnerable to the attack here made upon it. Dunbar v. United States, 156 U. S. 185, 191 et seq., 39 L. ed. 

390, 15 S. Ct. 325. Compare Pierce v. Creecy, 210 U. S. 387,

401, 402, 52 L. ed. 113, 28 S. Ct. 714; Ex parte Pierce (C. C.) 

155 F. 663, 665; United States v. Barber (D. C.) 157 F: 889, 891.

In view of this conclusion, it becomes unnecessary to consider the further question whether the trial court had jurisdiction to try the indictment, if construed as charging the commission of an offense only in Pennsylvania.

XIII.  71. The Pleas. 

The pleas, of which one¹ must be pleaded by a defendant who cannot successfully impugn the validity of the indictment against him, are either (1) General Pleas, that is, Guilty or Not Guilty, the latter called the general issue, or (2) Special Pleas, of which the most important, and in some jurisdictions the only ones available,³ are the pleas of Former Jeopardy and Pardon. 

72. A Plea of Guilty. 

A plea of guilty is a confession of the facts alleged by the indictment and a waiver of all formal defects therein,¹ and warrants the court to pass sentence upon the defendant with the same effect as if the allegations of the indictment had been found true by the verdict of a jury. Such a plea does not, however, establish that the facts alleged constitute a crime, nor preclude the accused to dispute the legal sufficiency of the charge. Upon the offering of this plea 2

73. Not Guilty. 

Not Guilty is a plea, called the general issue, which denies the criminal liability of the accused. It operates, therefore, as a traverse of the allegations made in the indictment, putting the prosecutor upon proof of the facts alleged, and also as a plea in confession and avoidance, enabling the defendant to avail himself of nearly all defenses which admit the facts alleged but rebut them by other facts which render the accused guiltless or not subject to punishment in the present prosecutor. Thus, it may be shown under this plea that, however true may be the averments of the indictment, the court is without jurisdiction to entertain the charge, or that, whatever the defendant did, he had legal excuse or justification for his action, such as self-defence for an assault or a homicide, or that the libel imputed to him was a true statement, or that the sales charged as illicit were made under a license. So this plea enables the accused to prove his insanity when doing the things charged, or that such things occurred so long ago that prosecution for them is barred by the Statute of Limitations. Indeed, the only defences not always available under the general issue are a former jeopardy and a pardon, and some cases hold that even these may, in certain conditions at least, be relied upon without being specially pleaded.⁹ 4 Accordingly, while a number of pleas setting up specially various defences such as limitations, insanity and the like -occur in the reports without reprobation, it is quite generally held that such special pleas are improper and should not be permitted except for the exceptional defences mentioned above.10

to be brought into jeopardy of his life more than once for the same offence." The same principle is embodied in the Fifth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States in these words, "No person shall be subject for the same offence to be twice put in jeopardy of life or limb." The constitutions of nearly (or quite) all of the American States contain like provisions in the same or similar forms of expression, which are, with only a few exceptions, of identical effect. Although the letter of the Constitutional enactment seems to confine its application to offences of which the punishment is death or mutilation, it is generally understood as extending to all offences of whatever gravity and to forbid a second prosecution for felony and misdemeanor alike. 2 is The Jeopardy contemplated by the Constitutional provisions, as their language is interpreted by a large majority of the courts, the peril of punishment which inheres in being placed on trial upon a criminal charge. The meaning is that a person, once tried upon such a charge, shall not be subjected to a second trial on account of the same offence. The prohibition, it will be observed, is not conditioned upon the outcome of the first trial, whether there be a verdict of conviction or of acquittal or no verdict at all, or upon the manner wherein that trial is conducted, whether correctly or otherwise. The Effect, therefore, is that, subject to certain qualifications to be later developed,5 when one has been once put upon trial, he must not be again exposed to the same peril on the same account, whether he be convicted or acquitted, or although the verdict rendered result from errors committed by the court or the prosecutor, or although, for any reason not of necessity and for which the defendant is not responsible, the trial have terminated without a verdict for or against him.

75. A Special Plea. 

A special plea is, at common law and in most jurisdictions,¹ requisite to assert that immunity against further prosecution which accrues from being once put upon trial. If in the original prosecution the accused has been found guilty by the verdict, and judgment has been entered thereon, he may plead in bar of a subsequent indictment alleging the same offence that he has been formerly convicted thereof, a plea of autrefois convict. 

If the former trial has resulted in a verdict of acquittal, he may, though judgment has not been entered on the verdict, plead to a later charge of the same offence that he has at another time been acquitted thereof, which is called the plea of autrefois acquit.* In the third possible case, that is, where the accused has once been put upon trial, before a jury or other tribunal competent to make a valid conviction, but the trial has been for some reason terminated before a verdict was reached, so that there is neither conviction nor acquittal, neither of the pleas just mentioned is literally appropriate, and neither apparently available. If in such a situation it is sought to subject the defendant to the hazard of a second trial, his proper mode of setting up that he has once been in jeopardy is a matter whereon there has been some diversity of judicial opinion and in respect of which there is some difference in the practice. Some courts have held that under the ordinary plea of autrefois acquit, it may be shown that the accused has once been placed on trial, the breakdown of that proceeding being deemed equivalent to an acquittal. other jurisdictions it is necessary to frame a special plea setting forth the former trial and its untimely termination, recounting the circumstances in which and for which the trial was brought to a close. Such a special plea may be, and sometimes is, called simply a plea of Former Jeopardy. 

76. Jeopardy Attaches.

In 

Jeopardy attaches to the accused when he is brought to trial (1) in a court of competent jurisdiction, (2) upon an indictment sufficient to sustain a conviction, and (3) a jury has been sworn to try the charge against him. Until these three things concur, there is no jeopardy in the legal sense of the term. Accordingly, one is not jeopardised by being brought before a magistrate for preliminary

Until that time a pending prosecution may be abandoned, as by a nolle pros. of an indictment, and a second prosecution may be instituted, as by bringing a new indictment, without subjecting the accused to a second jeopardy.

But when a person is once placed on trial before a jury sworn to try the accusation against him, the other constituents of jeopardy being present, he is entitled to insist that the trial proceed to a verdict of conviction or acquittal; and if, for any reason not amounting to necessity, the trial is terminated, without his consent or unless on account of his fault, before a verdict is had, he cannot again be brought to trial upon the same charge, since that would be to put him again in jeopardy.

Thus, a second trial is a violation of the defendant's constitutional immunity if, after the impanelling of a jury the prosecutor should nol. pros. the indictment, or if at his instance or for some other reason the trial should be abandoned and the jury discharged without giving a verdict, there being none of the facts intervening which the law recognises as sufficient to warrant such discharge. So if the indictment is one upon which the defendant might have been convicted, but the trial results in an acquittal, as from some erroneous ruling of the court or because some necessary witness is absent, the verdict protects the accused against a second trial for the same offence stated in another indictment or prosecuted in more favorable circumstances.8

PEREMPTORY PLEAS- —FORMER JEOPARDY 

539 10 judge or one of the judges was disqualified to officiate, or if the court was held at a place where it was not authorised to act, or if the court was not empowered by law to try such cases as that against the defendant, or if the cause was tried in a county other than that in which the alleged offence was committed," there having been no valid change of venue. If the plea fails to show that the former proceeding was in a court of competent jurisdiction, or if a prima facie showing of that jurisdiction is rebutted by proof of some such defect as has been instanced, it cannot be found that the defendant was legally in jeopardy when before put upon trial, and he is liable to further prosecution.' 12 The Indictment upon which the defendant was tried in the prior proceeding must, by the common law rule and the doctrine generally prevailing, appear to have been sufficient to sustain a conviction. 

This rule requires an indictment which would be held good upon a motion in arrest of judgment. The Effect of this doctrine is that, after one has been acquitted upon trial, if the prosecuting officer can discover a substantial defect in the indictment used, he may institute a second prosecution of the accused upon the same facts, and perhaps obtain a conviction, upon a corrected indictment; or if a trial has been launched, and the prosecutor finds that he has not the testimony available which is necessary to convict, he may nol. pros. the charge or withdraw a juror, with the right to renew the prosecution should he be able to disclose a flaw in the original indictment. As the pleading thus impeached is usually the handiwork of the prosecuting officer himself, such practice is very like enabling him to take advantage of his own wrong, and is also apt to prove oppressive upon those charged with crime. In view of such considerations, the Federal courts have (since 1896) refused to follow the common law doctrine, and hold that, where one has been acquitted after a trial of the merits, a second prosecution for the same offence may not be maintained against him upon the ground merely that the first proceeded upon a defective indictment.23 22 accrues.

27 before,26 and not afterwards, it being generally held that it is not necessary that any testimony be given or other action supervene after swearing of the jury.28 The accused becoming in jeopardy at that point, the trial must proceed to a verdict; and if it does not, a second trial cannot be had without creating a second jeopardy. 

And if a verdict is obtained, whether of guilt or of innocence, that verdict, unless vacated at the instance of the defendant, will preclude another trial on the same charge, although the finding is the result of error committed at the trial or of some accident for which the accused was not responsible.

Accordingly, if after swearing of the jury, the trial is abandoned, as by entry of a nol. pros., 29 or by withdrawal of a juror,30 or by an unwarranted discharge of the jury, the defendant, when again indicted or again brought to trial on the same charge may successfully plead that he has once been in jeopardy. And if upon the trial so commenced, he is acquitted through an erroneous ruling of the court or by a defect of proof, he is not, by reason of such miscarriage, to be subjected to the jeopardy of a second trial for the same offence.

78. Waiver of Immunity.

Where one found guilty of a crime procures judgment upon the verdict to be arrested,¹ or applies for and obtains a new trial,2 or upon writ of error or appeal causes the judgment to be reversed and the verdict vacated, there is on the part of the defendant so moving an express or implied consent to a second trial, which amounts to a waiver of his immunity on account of the jeopardy created by the first trial. In such cases, therefore, it does not violate the Constitutional prohibition of second jeopardy to retry the accused upon the same charge.

Appeal by the State from the judgment upon a verdict acquitting the accused must have for its object a vacation of the verdict and a second trial of the same charge. But that would contravene the rule against second jeopardy; and it is therefore something which, in all but one or two of the States, no court, whether of original

Partial Acquittal. One who is wholly acquitted of the charge against him is not likely to seek a second trial, either by moving for a new trial or by writ of error or appeal. One accused of a certain crime may, however, be convicted of that crime in a less degree than is charged or of some offence included in that charged; as where on indictment for murder in the first degree the defendant is found guilty of murder in the second degree or of manslaughter or of assault and battery, or on a charge of assault with intent to rob or to ravish there is a verdict finding only the assault and not the aggravating intent." In any such cases the verdict is a virtual acquittal of so much of the accusation as exceeds the offence of which guilt is found. If, now, the culprit obtains upon motion a new trial, or upon writ of error a reversal of the conviction, which reversal, in the usual case, directs a second trial, the question arises, whether at the second trial the defendant is liable to be convicted of the whole offence charged, or is he, as to all the excess above the crime first found, protected by his former jeopardy, which covered that excess and as to which he has been acquitted? "This question has given rise to much diversity of opinion in the various State courts."12 13 By the common law an acquittal of murder bars a later prosecution for manslaughter upon the same person, "because the latter charge is included in the former;" and e converso acquittal of manslaughter will preclude a future prosecution for the murder of the same person. The same principle is approved by "the general consensus of American textbooks on criminal law and the overwhelming weight of American decided cases." Accordingly, in most of the States, if a person accused of a larger crime, as murder, be convicted of a minor offence necessarily included in that charged, as manslaughter or a lower degree of murder, and the conviction be reversed with direction for a retrial, the defendant can on the second trial be convicted of no offence exceeding in gravity that where- 

Pa. 380, 185 Atl. 498; other cases in note 8. 

11. It is not necessary for the prosecution to prove the accused guilty of the whole wrongdoing charged, and "it is sufficient to prove so much of the indictment as shows that the defendant has committed a substantive crime therein specified:" 1 Chitty Crim. L. 

250, where numerous examples are stated: Hudson v. S., 1 Blackford, 318; Stewart v. S., 5 Ohio, 242; S. v. 

Stedman, 7 Porter, 495; C. v. Cooper, 15 Mass. 187. Hence there may be a conviction of any minor offence which is necessarily included in that which is charged, provided of course that the elements of the minor offence are set forth in the indictment: 1 Chitty 

[Cases in Crim. Proc.]-35 

Crim. L. 250, and instances there given. But the minor offence must be sufficiently charged as part of the larger: thus on an indictment for murder, there can be no conviction of involuntary manslaughter: C. V. 

Gable, 7 S. & R. 423.

of he was convicted, having once been in jeopardy as to the residue of the crime alleged.15

In a number of other States and in the Federal courts is a different doctrine, according to which a successful application to vacate a verdict finding the accused guilty of an included offence or an effective appeal to secure reversal of the judgment entered upon such a verdict, reopens the whole question of the defendant's guilt, and upon retrial he may be convicted of the entire charge, without benefit from the partial acquittal implied by the former verdict.16 

In still other States, by the constitutions or by statutes, it is enacted that the granting of a new trial, on motion or upon writ of error, shall place the parties in the same position as if no former trial had taken place. The effect of this and like provisions is to adopt the second of the doctrines just stated, and to render one, who has been but partially convicted, and by implication acquitted of greater criminality, liable upon another trial to be found guilty of the whole crime for which he was originally tried.17 

79. Identity of Offences. 

To sustain a plea of former jeopardy, it must appear that the of fence for which the defendant was previously tried was the identical offence with which he is charged by the second indictment,¹ and for which the prosecution intends to subject him to a second trial. The two offences must be the same both in fact and in law.

IDENTITY IN LAW. Unless two indictments allege violations of the same law, a trial upon one cannot be successfully pleaded as a jeopardy barring trial upon the other. This is because a single act may be prohibited by two or more laws, and so of itself constitute two or more offences.

Two Sovereignties may make the same act a crime against each of them. Thus, the sale of certain articles may be declared unlawful by a statute of the United States and also by a statute of a State.¹4 

So the making and the issue of counterfeit money is made criminal by a Federal statute and is also a violation of the statutory or common law of most States.15 For such forbidden acts the offender may be prosecuted under the law of the United States and also under the law of the State, and a conviction or an acquittal in one of these prosecutions is not a jeopardy which bars a trial in the other.16 

Some other things are sometimes prohibited by a statute of a State and also by an ordinance of a municipality within the State; and in such condition of the law it is (generally) held that a prosecution under the ordinance does not preclude prosecution under the statute and vice versa. 17 18 So, as has been seen, an act done in one State may violate the law of another State; in which case a trial in one of the States does not prevent trial for the same offence in the other. 19

Two Provisions of Law, common law or statutory, adopted or enacted by the same State, may severally prohibit the same thing when done in differing ways or in various circumstances; whereby a person is made, by a single act, an offender against both, or possibly more than two, prohibitions.20 In that state of the law, the fact

80. Included Offences. 

A conviction or an acquittal upon the charge of a crime which necessarily includes¹ minor offences is a bar to further prosecution of any of the minor offences; as if one be indicted for murder in the first degree, the verdict had upon a trial, or the discharge of the jury without good cause before a verdict arrived at (sec. 77, ante), will prevent a subsequent trial for murder in a lower degree, for manslaughter or for assault and battery alleged as committed in the same homicide. E converso, a conviction of one of the offences included in the larger crime will, unless the verdict be vacated at the instance of the defendant (sec. 78, ante), preclude a later prosecution for any of the higher grades of crime constituting the maximum guilt alleged; thus, a verdict finding the defendant guilty of manslaughter precludes a second jeopardy for any of the degrees of murder.2 So if the accusation is of an assault aggravated by some special criminal circumstance, as an intent to kill, to rob or to ravish, and the defendant is found guilty of only the simple assault, such a verdict will protect him against a sequent prosecution for murder, for robbery or for rape, occurring in the same affair; since the aggravating incidents are negatived by the verdict of guilty without the aggravation. 

1. It will be observed that, in all the instances adduced in exemplification of this rule, the larger crime is composed of one or more minor offences which must be committed in order to arrive at and consummate the greater. The rule, as also will be observed, does not apply where the less offence is not necessarily included in the larger, though each may have elements common to both; thus, a burglary may be committed without accomplishment of the intended felony, and one may steal, murder or ravish in a house without a prior burglary. A trial for murder, requiring proof of all the constituents of that crime, is therefore, a jeopardy as to the inferior offences; but a charge of burglary does not bar one of larceny or rape, because either crime may be proved independently of the (perhaps) actually concomitant elements of the other, and although the affair involved the commission of both crimes.

S. v.

Qualifications. This general principle is, however, subject to three qualifications. (a) It does not operate in all its fullness in a jurisdiction where guilt of the minor offence cannot be found upon a charge of the larger one; as where upon an indictment for felony it is not competent to convict of an included misdemeanor. If, the local law is so, one indicted for murder or manslaughter cannot be found guilty of assault and battery, or of an attempt to commit murder; and one indicted for assault with intent to kill, to rob or to ravish, if such assaults are felonies, cannot be convicted of simple assault. In such a jurisdiction an acquittal of the felony does not imply innocence of a possible misdemeanor committed in the affair alleged as a felony; wherefore the verdict is not a protection against an independent prosecution for an assault or other minor misconduct connected with the transaction adjudged not felonious. (b) Acquittal or conviction of a minor offence is not a bar to prosecution for a larger offence to which the minor was incident if the conviction or acquittal was had in a court which was without jurisdiction to try and convict one charged with the major crime. Thus, a prosecution for statutory rape is not precluded by conviction of an indecent assault upon the same girl, if the conviction was obtained in a municipal (or like inferior) court which is not competent to act upon charges of felony." (c) Trial for a less offence which may possibly be part of a greater is not a bar to trial for the major crime if the latter was not consummated when the accused was first tried. If, for example, one is convicted of assault and battery upon a person, who afterward dies of the injuries inflicted by the battery, the assailant is not, by the judgment had in the assault case, protected against a prosecution for murder. This doctrine is accounted for by saying that a new fact has supervened, the death creating a crime different from the assault and battery, a crime not completely committed until the death occurred, and one which requires other proof than was necessary in the original proceeding; and it is acccordingly conceived that the situation comes within the rule that two offences are not identical if they cannot be proved by the same evidence (sec. 79, ante). 

81. Plea of Pardon. A general pardon, often called an amnesty, may be granted by an act of the legislature or by a proclamation of the Executive, if (as is usual)¹ he possesses the power to pardon. Whether made by statute or by proclamation, the pardon is a public act, of which all courts must take notice in the ordinary administration of the law. It is, therefore, not necessary to plead such a pardon.

A special pardon is an act of the President or of the Governor, who executes with the solemnities requisite for such an official document, a writ declaring that some one or more persons therein named is or are pardoned for certain offences, of which conviction may or may not have been had. 

Advantage of a pardon in this form can be obtained only by a special plea ;* which, if it is to be pleaded in bar of conviction must be pleaded before a plea of the general issue; though the pardon may also be set up, after a verdict of guilty, in bar of a sentence. Even after the convict has been sentenced, he may (if he can) produce a pardon to prevent execution of the sentence or to procure his release from imprisonment.

Perovich, 274 U. S. 480, 71 L. ed. 1161, 47 S. Ct. 664. 

5. C. v. Lockwood, 109 Mass. 339. 

6. 4 Bl. Com. 402; C. v. Lockwood, supra.

v. Hartwell, 3. Cliff. 221, Fed. Cas. No. 15,318. Like a demurrer this plea admits, for the purposes of the case, all the facts which are well pleaded, but is not to be used as an admission elsewhere. Com. v. Tilton, 8 Metc. (Mass.) 232. Not available as an estoppel to a civil action. Com. v. Horton, 9 Pick. (Mass.) 206."

This plea is now of infrequent use in this state. It appears that it is in general practice in some of the New England states. 

In the case of Buck v. Commonwealth, 107 Pa. 486, it is said that: "The plea of nolo contendere is a mild form of pleading guilty." 

Mr. Bishop in his New Criminal Procedure, vol. 1, § 802, defines the plea as: "The defendant's declaration in court that he will not contend with the prosecuting power."

Discussing when the plea may be used and its effect, Mr. Bishop says in the same section: ors.
